ideas.th: AV market fragmenting beyond Waymo/Tesla makes Uber the aggregator; ~15x 2027 GAAP P/E is an all-time low.
ideas.cat: Driverless launches by Motional, May Mobility, Zoox on Uber
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Uber as a long.

The presenter thinks organic bookings can grow mid to high-teens and organic EPS mid-20%s over the next few years. The presenter is fairly in line (or slightly higher) with the Street on organic estimates, so this is more of a call on the current multiple.

The multiple is severely depressed for a quality franchise (~15x 2027 GAAP P/E which is an all-time low). Using a SOTP analysis, if you put their delivery business at a 20% discount to DoorDash, you are paying ~7.5x for their mobility business, which is not so far off of where Lyft, the number 2 player is trading, and very similar to where Expedia and Instacart are currently trading, which are also competitively-threatened marketplace businesses but grow at half the rate of UBER Mobility. So, the market is pricing their mobility business for a punitive case, and the whole company appears too cheap versus its growth.

The biggest reason for this is existential fears from autonomous vehicles, and the presenter thinks autonomous vehicle fears can start to get alleviated over the next 6 to 12 months, which should provide relief to the multiple.

Separately, the presenter likes that UBER is relatively insulated from AI fears versus most of their internet coverage. They provide a simpler and time-sensitive transaction that does not need agents, it is a physical fulfillment network that agents or AI cannot replicate, and it is not as heavily dependent on advertising for profitability as other marketplaces are. To be clear, there is a terminal value debate here, but it is one that has been known and capitalized for two years, and the presenter thinks the fear factor improves.

On the AV debate, the only thing that matters is whether or not the AV market fragments. Today, especially in the US, 100% of the driverless deployment in AVs are Waymo and Tesla, and the majority of that is on their own 1P apps. If Waymo and Tesla win the market long-term and only source demand on their own apps, that is clearly bad for Uber. But if AVs fragment beyond those two to a longer tail of partners, and they need Uber for demand generation, then AVs become a commodity and Uber is the go-to aggregator.

Right now, the presenter thinks Uber is priced as if Waymo and Tesla will take over the AV world, at the expense of Uber's network. But the presenter thinks it is increasingly likely that AVs fragment over the next few years for three reasons.

First, the technology is diffusing. There are several private AV companies that claim to have solved, or be close to solving, the Level 4 autonomous problem. The shocking part is that these companies have done it only raising anywhere from $500 million to $2 billion each, versus the tens of billions that Waymo has raised in funding.

You never know how much these private companies exaggerate the abilities of their technology, but things we at least know to be true are that hardware costs have come down meaningfully over the last 5 years - LiDAR, for instance, has come down 90%+ and AI advancements have made model training much more effective, reducing the need for having a fleet that goes out and physically maps every nook and cranny of a city. So, the presenter thinks the tech problem has lower barriers to solve today, and L4 tech is starting to diffuse. Second, there are proof points finally on the horizon that non-Waymo and Tesla AV players are figuring it out in terms of the US market. Driverless deployments are the key metric that ultimately matters with AVs. Waymo and Tesla are 100% of the commercial driverless AV deployments in the US today, and they are mostly doing it on their own 1P apps. But Uber has a few partners in the US that are targeting initial driverless deployments on Uber’s platform as early as Q4 of this year. Those three are Motional, May Mobility, and Zoox, and there are a few other partners that are targeting deployments in 2027. Essentially, once a couple of these long-tail partners have successful driverless deployments in the US, the presenter believes it will show that Waymo did not uniquely crack this problem, which will provide relief to the multiple.

Third is international (ex-China), which is importantly over half of the mobility business for Uber. That market is already fragmenting on AVs, and the presenter thinks that is underappreciated. Waymo and Tesla have zero commercial driverless deployments in international markets. Important to note, the market leaders in International are in fact Uber's partners, not their competitors. The Chinese AV players are the ones who lead international (ex-China) deployments, and they are choosing to partner with the large rideshare players (outside of China). The added benefit in international is that Europe and Japan are the two biggest viable markets for AVs outside of the US, simply given the pricing in those markets. There has been a lot of regulatory red tape in terms of commercial deployments in those markets, and those regulatory bottlenecks have resulted in a more level playing field / fragmented playing field, where a host of other players are catching up on the technology side before any one player has scaled on deployments.

In terms of ring-fencing the real disruption fears, the presenter thinks it is most valid for Uber's US mobility business, which will only be 25% to 30% of the group's Pro Forma EBITDA in 2028. The presenter thinks the AV fear is only relevant within large markets in the US, which will account for approximately 15% of Uber's EBITDA in 2028.

In terms of the catalyst path, the main catalyst is simply getting driverless deployments from the long tail of UBER AV partners in the US, possibly as early as this quarter, but more than likely you will see multiple players doing so in 2027. Then the real deployment scaling of that long tail comes in 2028. The presenter does not think most investors think much of the long tail of AV partners today. Uber has 20+ partners, they are difficult to track, and, in the presenter’s opinion, nobody knows if they are legitimate or not. Having a couple of partners with a technological breakthrough, the presenter thinks, will matter a lot for the multiple. On the risk-reward, if the presenter gets evidence that the AV terminal debate is not as bad as feared and there is no real AI debate, they think this could easily re-rate to a low 20s multiple on GAAP P/E. That would equate to a target price of $95-$100 versus the current share price of $70. At that valuation, UBER is trading at less than a 1x PEG, which is in-line with large-cap tech peers.

In a downside case scenario, you would see the mobility segment become a no-growth runoff business, that loses pricing power, loses volume to Tesla and Waymo, and essentially gets priced at 4x EBITDA. That would equate to a $55 share price, or approximately 20% downside from current levels. The presenter thinks the upside could be in the low $100s, so 60%+. The presenter likes the skew and thinks the catalysts over the next six months on alleviating the AV fears are interesting.

ideas.th: Bookings well ahead of revenue and AI copper business durable; mid-teens multiple should move toward 20x with buybacks.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss TE Connectivity as a long.

Bookings have been growing very quickly. It is a mid-teens multiple business which generates a lot of free cash flow. They have an AI business that is 20% to 25% of business. It is copper-focused. There is a secular bear case against copper when you look out 3 to 5 years, that copper is going to be replaced by fiber. The presenter also likes Corning (GLW) and they think both stocks likely work from current levels. The presenter thinks the transition from copper to fiber is simply going to take longer than expected.

In the presenter’s opinion, the CEO is frustrated because the company has an industrial business that is trading at a significant discount to industrial peers, because they sold everybody on AI expectations. That said, the AI business, DDN, is 20% of the business. Bookings have been very strong, so there has been a large gap between bookings and revenue growth. For reference, the company missed last quarter, but the presenter thinks that was caused simply by the lumpiness of the business. The presenter thinks you have that hit this quarter. It is a lumpy business, and the presenter believes it is a legacy industrial company that is not as accustomed to talking to tech investors. Now the CEO is pulling back on disclosures as the presenter believes he does not like the AI business, even though his AI business is doing quite well.

The presenter thinks there is upside to numbers and upside to the current multiple. If AI comes back into vogue, there will be upside from that perspective also. Approximately 40% to 45% of the business is auto. It makes sensors and connectors, [and is] China-levered in the China EV business. It also has some exposure to European autos from a China competitive perspective, but the presenter thinks they are capturing what they lose from a market-share perspective.

In summary, it is an industrial name that is trading at a mid-teens multiple, that should be trading closer to a 20x multiple, with a material stock buyback. The setup provides a compelling risk-reward with a lot of optionality should AI ever come back into vogue. Frankly, who knows where sentiment goes from here and whether these IPOs get done or not. But some of these businesses, in the presenter's opinion, are pretty durable.

ideas.th: No new HDD supply before 2029, HAMR lead and rising $/TB; 7x presenter's $92 FY28 EPS, with a large buyback likely.
ideas.cat: $10B+ buyback expected on next earnings call
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Seagate as a long.

In terms of the setup, the entire memory complex is completely out of favor. The stock is down 42% from the June high of $1,100, 32% of that since the beginning of the month, and that is after two Toshiba headlines as well as the general AI sell-off.

According to the presenter’s work, every number in the business has gone up. At $640, Seagate trades at 7x the presenter's FY28 number of EPS, which is $92, and 10x the Street, which is $60. This is a peak-earnings multiple for a business whose next six to eight quarters are already sold out and priced, in an industry where nobody can add drive capacity before 2029.

The presenter's base-case valuation is $1,000. The real risk is a 2023-style cut in cloud spending in 2028 and 2029, and not Toshiba. Why it works is, there is no new supply before 2029. Industry exabyte growth only comes from putting more data on each disk, because there is a limited number of disks that can be created across the three players. The two parts that set capacity - recording heads and disks - take approximately two years to add. Management says demand is above supply and the gap is widening. The presenter thinks it is up 2,000 exabytes this year, demand is over 3,000, and that gap is widening next year. Seagate also has the technology lead amongst all of its competitors. They make their drives using this technology called HAMR, which is heat-assisted magnetic recording. This puts a tiny laser in the head that heats a spot on the disk so that bits can be packed more tightly. HAMR is how drive capacity goes from 30 terabytes to 40 terabytes, and then 50 terabytes onwards. HAMR is expected to be 80% to 90% of data center volume in a few years, and this is the only way in which you can get more exabytes in the same number of disks.

Western Digital has been trying to move onto HAMR for years now. They finally might be able to do it next year; they are going to provide an update on whether they can do it next quarter. Additionally, Toshiba (a 10% player) recently came out with a headline that said they want to move to 30% market share in three years. The presenter can go over the details as to why they think that is a highly improbable scenario.

In terms of pricing, the presenter believes Seagate’s price per terabyte was up +11% in the last quarter. On management calls, if you do checks, they are basically saying $25 per terabyte can move higher. The presenter recently talked to one of the neo-clouds and they believe they paid around $35 per terabyte last quarter and can look to potentially pay over $40 per terabyte in the next year. So, prices are still rising. Gross margin was 53% in June. It is not like the 80-85% that you see in memory; so, the presenter thinks there is still a lot of headway for those margins to move higher, which is why the presenter disagrees with the idea that earnings have peaked.

Given the demand visibility, and the fact that you need more passive data to be stored in HDDs, the presenter sees it extremely unlikely where you would not need more HDD capacity. In the presenter’s opinion, users don’t delete data. They simply store more data. Essentially, that is what is happening on the data center side as well. There are very few amounts of data that actually get deleted in the cloud; it is not like a first-in, first-out type of situation. When you have the advent of physical AI robots, you are going to have even more training datasets, in the form of video, that are hundreds of hundreds of gigabytes of data that need to be stored on these HDDs.

Lastly, Western Digital has been doing buybacks in earnest, while Seagate has not started an expansive buyback program (they have been retiring their high-coupon debt instead). The last note that they retired was a ~9% note. Management has flagged higher buybacks in 2027 and a dividend review. Only $4 billion is left on the $5 billion authorization, which equates to only 3% of the market cap so far, against $18 billion of free cash flow expected in CY 27. The presenter believes you are going to see a massive buyback authorization coming from Seagate. The presenter expects $10 billion+ to be announced during the next earnings call.

ideas.th: Odyssey-driven 2026 EBITDA won't repeat; 13x EBITDA vs <10x history and takeout hopes fade after CEO's $50M sale.

ideas.th: Lagging-node capacity tightening brings pricing gains while mix shifts to auto/data center; TSM and Japan deals add optionality.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss GlobalFoundries as a long.

Earlier this year, there was a lot of optimism in lagging-node foundry as TSM pulled back capacity since it is no longer economical for TSM to invest in those nodes. This has made the foundry market in older nodes tighter (UMC’s stock went up dramatically as well on similar dynamics).

GFS followed suit, and they were trying to play second fiddle to Tower Semi - TSEM, not TSM - in silicon photonics. And then you had a cavalcade of quantum-vibe headlines, and the stock went from $35 to $90, even though they never beat numbers. The stock has subsequently traded back to the mid-$40s.

So, what happened? Investors realized that their silicon photonics ambitions were meaningfully worse than Tower Semi’s, which the presenter believes to be true. There is more competition; STMicroelectronics is also in that market, and there are other players. So why now? The presenter was turning more bullish on the name even before a few recent headlines. The high-level view is that going into next year, the overall semis ecosystem is going to become materially tighter, including in lagging node. Most of these companies built out a lot of capacity during the pandemic. Then demand died and no one built out capacity for a few years. The AI spillover effect is utilizing a lot of that excess capacity, and then into next year it is expected to be even tighter, pushing up pricing. The presenter sees that pricing is likely going to be a mid-single-digit / high-single-digit contributor to growth next year for a business that historically sees price coming down. The presenter believes that you will likely see a similar dynamic in 2028 as well.

And then, interestingly, the business is in transition. It has historically been highly leveraged to the smartphone market (the presenter believes it peaked at almost half the business a few years ago). Smartphones are now down to low 30% today, and it should go to sub-20% in the presenter's forecast period (exiting 2028 or so). The growth is coming from a combination of auto (they have been winning new business with mostly European players over the last few years) and from the other growth segment which is data center. They also have some satellite exposure. Interestingly enough, they picked up a win with Monolithic Power, a fabless semiconductor company that the presenter is also bullish on.

Most recently, in the last few weeks, there have been some positive headlines. TSM announced a $2 billion deal with GFS to provide, starting in 2029, on substrates. And last week, the presenter saw a headline where the Japanese government is co-investing with the US government, where GFS will be acting as an outsourced fab manager. They are not actually going to be operating the fab; they are essentially helping and building IP. There is no CAPEX associated with it. They are going to start generating management fees starting next year. Then over time, they will generate an actual EBITDA share.

The presenter thinks these deals are signifying, beyond the fact that GFS is becoming a pseudo-real foundry, that the environment is becoming materially tighter. These deals would not have been signed if the companies looking at all this ecosystem of 2028, 2029, and beyond did not see that this market being very tight. GFS would have never gotten a look. And so, the presenter thinks that it is emblematic of their original thesis, that the stock had fully round tripped.

The valuation is also attractive. The Street is underwriting EPS of $3.40. In 2028, the presenter is $1 higher, assigning a low double-digit multiple. The presenter thinks a reasonable valuation is mid to high teens (if they can execute), which equates to a $65 or $70 price target. In summary, the end market is tight and it is going to get tighter, and pricing is going to improve. You have a couple of interesting out-year optionality deals with TSM and with the Japanese and US governments. That is out-year optionality in the presenter's view, as the company is structurally improving from an end-market mix perspective - less from consumer and more from auto, data centers, as well as better end markets.

ideas.th: Koch/GC preferred values Axiom spin at $30-37.5B, implying RemainCo at 1.5-7x EBIT; re-rating to 10x gives 20-40% upside.
ideas.cat: November Investor Day; Axiom spin-off in Q1 2027
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Flex as a long.

Flex has a $39 billion enterprise value and a $33 billion market cap.

The presenter believes the stock is trading at an attractive entry point at $87 per share. It is an EMS, that is spinning off its AI power and cloud business from its Remain Co (broader contract manufacturing segment plus networking). Their AI power and cloud business, called Axiom, is projected to grow 70% in 2027 (which has a March fiscal year end) and accelerate next year. Flex is spinning off Axiom in Q1 2027.

It is interesting now because they recently bought a company called EPC Power that has leading equipment for 800-volt DC architecture and know-how around it. To help close the deal, they had Koch Industries and General Catalyst invest $2 billion in a preferred at an implied enterprise value for the Axiom spin-off of $37.5 billion. It is really a range of $30 to $37.5 billion, but against the current enterprise value of $39 billion, there is some dislocation in valuation, because it implies that the Remain Co trades anywhere from 1.5x to 7x adjusted EBIT, and no comp in the peer group trades nearly that cheaply. If the Remain Co is worth 10x and the spin-off is $30 billion to $37.5 billion, which would equate to 11.5x to 13x adjusted EBIT, a re-rating to 10x on the Remain Co would equate to 20% to 40% upside. Important to note, they have an Investor Day in November. The perception the presenter gets is that there is a preference for Jabil at the moment, because they have Helios exposure, and investors are questioning the catalytic nature of the November Investor Day - whether it will in fact be a catalyst - because they have not spun off Axiom, and they may be limited in what they can say. But in terms of the setup, the presenter believes it is a stock that investors will “chase” to own, and want to own, as you exit this year and into next year.

ideas.th: Rising compute prices and hard-to-build capacity accrue to existing assets; renewal pricing and high-margin interconnect drive upside.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Equinix as a long.

In terms of the setup, the presenter thinks there is 40% upside from current levels. That is low $50s per share of AFFO (Adjusted Funds From Operations) next year, assigning a high-20s multiple on that, or approximately a low-20s EBITDA multiple (22x or 23x).

The premise of the thesis is that the presenter believes compute prices go materially higher next year, and only higher after that. The presenter also believes that it will become much more difficult to build (financing is clearly a concern, as well as regulatory and permitting concerns). All that value accrues to steel in the ground / existing assets. Equinix has a meaningful footprint in the US, with 30% of that coming up for contract renewal next year, and the presenter thinks that there is headroom for them to take double-digit pricing on that portion of the business.

Then you have the cross-connect opportunity, which allows them to effectively connect siloed and secure pockets of data directly within their data center. The presenter thinks this is flowing through at super high incremental margins (80% to 90%+). This is a primary winner of the inference compute trend, and as inference workloads go higher, interconnect should follow thereafter.

On a risk-reward basis, in this type of tape the presenter thinks it is quite attractive, where you have a large contracted base of compute signed, and then you get the upside optionality. It is relatively less capital intensive than some of the neo-clouds, while still retaining some of that spot exposure. In this type of more defensive AI tape, it is an interesting risk-reward opportunity.

ideas.th: Speed matters less than token cost; ~85% customer concentration, OpenAI dependence and 39% GM guide don't justify 19x 2028.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Cerebras as a short.

Most investors are aware of the story, but the company’s pitch is that they can produce chips that can run 10 to 20 times faster than Nvidia’s. The important aspect to the story is understanding the technology behind it. The KV (Key-Value) cache is something that gets bigger the more you use an LLM. Cerebras keeps model weights and working memory in on-wafer SRAM, right next to the compute. What they deliver is 1,000 times a single GPU's HBM bandwidth. They can generate 2,100 tokens per second versus approximately 130 on the fastest GPU service in its published Llama-70B benchmark. Less time moving data means much faster inference.

Its architecture can deliver dramatically faster answers, but the question is, is it a good business, and does that speed actually matter? The presenter believes that faster does not matter much for the vast majority of workloads, and the presenter believes that all the focus is on token cost at the moment (not absolute speed).

For background, the IPO took forever to accomplish. The person that is running the company is a wonderful CEO, but the presenter thinks he is promotional. His pitch is, “this is faster than Nvidia,” and the presenter thinks that narrative caught hold, particularly within the retail investment community.

In terms of the business, they are not selling a GPU; they are selling a complex system. There is material customer concentration risk, as four customers account for ~85% of revenue, and just two of them account for 76% of accounts receivable. OpenAI is a substantial portion of the revenue ramp that the entire valuation rests on, because the Street thinks EPS goes from a $0.47 loss this year, to a $1.30 gain next year, and in 2028 (the big earnings ramp year), the Street is underwriting $6.47 in EPS.

If you look at where the stock is trading, it is trading at approximately 19x 2028. Previously, the Street was underwriting $5.50 (only a few months ago), but analysts have raised their estimates after the deal announcement with AWS (although no numbers or dates have been disclosed regarding this deal with AWS).

Important to note, they recently guided gross margin down to only 39%. Nvidia's operating margin is higher than that, yet Cerebras trades at a higher multiple (Nvidia trades at 13.7x 2028).

The presenter thinks they only generate EPS of $5.50, and using an 18x multiple for Cerebras, that would equate to a price target of $99. For reference, the stock is currently trading at ~$120 per share. The presenter thinks it could unravel faster than that. One final point, the deal with OpenAI does not allow them to sell this to other competitors. So how big could it really be?

The presenter believes that any hiccup in OpenAI spending could unwind this rather quickly.

ideas.th: Auto restocking, data-center pricing power and rising rack/800V content; $2.50 EPS vs Street <$2 plus a humanoid call option.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Allegro MicroSystems as a long.

For background, the company provides unique sensing technology and analog devices, with 65% of their sales from the auto market, a mid to high-teens percentage of their sales from data center, and the remainder dispersed between markets like traditional industrial, clean energy, and robotics.

Near-term, the presenter believes that investors are underappreciating their growth trajectory in the automotive market despite broader profit warnings at OEMs. The prolonged semiconductor inventory correction seems to be improving a bit. Relative to even last quarter, various distributors and semiconductor vendors are sounding incrementally more positive on order activity and restocking in the automotive market, given Tier 1s have been holding extremely lean inventory for quite a while.

Secondly, as data center demand creates capacity constraints, you are seeing broader analog, and Allegro itself, having the power to increase pricing. So, the presenter expects the company to benefit from second-half pricing increases and favorable negotiating terms with auto customers as contracts roll off in 2027. They typically see low-to-single-digit declines at the start of the year in terms of pricing, but the presenter thinks they can likely maintain flat or up pricing.

And then in the medium to longer term, you have the introduction of new products such as isolated gate drivers that can expand their SAM (Serviceable Addressable Market) per vehicle by 2x. On top of this, Allegro has a strong data center portfolio that should outperform conservative expectations of growing in line with CAPEX. Initial products were for motor drivers, fans, and air-cooling applications, which should continue to grow as we see adoptions in areas like power supplies. But the portfolio is shifting towards current sensors that help in current measuring and fault detection, which is a faster growth and higher-margin area for the company.

They have outlined $150 of content per rack growing to $425 by 2028. The SAM per rack is improving, and that does not account for the full extent of the shift to 800-volt architecture, which could add hundreds of dollars to the SAM on top of that. In the presenter’s opinion, they will also be introducing isolated gate drivers into that market.

The last point - and this is more of a call option that is not embedded in estimates - is centered around physical AI. In terms of the humanoid opportunity, Allegro is likely the largest pure play there. Growth in factory robotics near-term is beneficial, but broader robotics is only 3% or 4% of sales currently. Allegro has the portfolio to provide several TMR sensors in the robotic hand, and they believe they will see $150 SAM per humanoid. It is not embedded in estimates, but this number is 3x current factory robots that they service which creates an opportunity beyond 2028.

In summary, with near-term cyclical trends improving and pricing power strong, combined with this long-term call option, it feels that the current share price is too conservative. The presenter models EPS exiting closer to $2.50 versus the Street below $2.00, which implies Allegro is trading two standard deviations below its mean. Even trading one standard deviation below on the presenter's numbers equate to 40% upside, and investors can certainly go up from there. Then you have the call option that investors focus on physical AI into 2027. That is why the presenter believes that the risk-reward profile is attractive.

ideas.th: Backlog up ~90% points to 2027 acceleration vs Street deceleration; China WFE winner at mid-single-digit FY28 P/E.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss ACM Research as a long.

Hypothetically, what if investors could invest in a stock where the end customers do not really care about CoreWeave yields or how the US labs are doing. It is an AI winner, and it is also trading at a very cheap mid-single-digit P/E multiple on FY28 earnings. It is also growing top line north of 30% CAGR over the next few years.

The company is based in Fremont, California. It trades on the Nasdaq (it is not an ADR). They are levered to CXMT and YMTC expansion in China, and they also have gross margins in the mid-40%s. For those who are unfamiliar, ACM Research is an equipment supplier. A vast majority of their revenue serves the Chinese market. They recently printed backlog up almost 90% year over year.

The Street believes revenue will decelerate in 2027 to mid-20s percent growth from roughly 30% this year. Given the backlog and the potential for international expansion (they are looking to sell more tools outside of China), as well as new product lines, the presenter believes that their growth will materially accelerate next year. If investors track backlog over the last several years and then the year-forward revenue, they map very closely. The largest delta in recent history was approximately 11%. But if you look at the Street assumptions for 2027 revenue and the delta from the backlog that they just printed, it is over 60% (quite a large disparity). For reference, for the first half of 2026, the company's backlog was up over 100% year over year.

The presenter also thinks the company is progressing well in its cleaning business (their main business), where they compete against players like Naura and Kingsemi in China. They have majority share, and they are also making notable inroads in other markets like ECP copper plating, advanced packaging and panel-level packaging, furnace, thermal processing, and PECVD as well.

The presenter believes this opportunity exists because investors were historically worried about two factors. Number one, gross margins, and they were worried that they would compress as they introduced new product areas. But gross margins have held. Number two, investors would question why this company is undergrowing WFE this year? That is why the presenter thinks the opportunity exists. In the presenter’s opinion, once it becomes clearer that they will accelerate next year, the market will likely assign a better multiple on the stock.

The presenter is underwriting ~$6 in EPS in 2027 and thinks it should trade at a 20x multiple, equating to a price target of $120. It is currently trading at $55, so the presenter thinks it is a double over the next year.

ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Zip as a short.

Zip is an Australian buy-now-pay-later platform. Zip trade son the ASX, but most of their business and pretty much all of their growth comes from the United States, where they run the fourth or fifth-largest buy-now-pay-later platform, branded Zip. In the presenter’s view, this is one of the least differentiated buy-now-pay-later players and they are new to the US market.

Up until 2022, they were effectively a roll-up of international buy-now-pay-later platforms, particularly in Saudi Arabia and Singapore. They ended up divesting all of those assets and fired their CEO, in the presenter’s opinion. Also worth noting, the presenter believes they are serial re-staters; every time the business slows down, they take off a metric or re-state a metric. Today, in the US, their customer growth has severely stalled from around mid-teens to mid-single digits, and AOV is flat and declining.

What is driving growth in the US business today is transaction frequency. They are working with the same cohort of customers and getting them to spend more on Zip’s platform, buying not just their electric scooters on Zip, but also their groceries, for example. To maintain that growth, they launched a new product called “Pay in 8”—which doubles the amount of time a customer can take to pay off their loans versus the previous “Pay in 4”—and in tandem changed their definition of a customer default to also be twice as long. In the presenter’s opinion, they have masked the fact that they are now making lower-quality loans to boost growth (somewhere close to where it used to be).

The company trades on a cash EBITDA multiple, which adds back the provision for loss accruals, which is another questionable practice regarding this business. If you reverse the add-back, it trade sat approximately 25x EBITDA, which is well above comps that trade around 20x. Even at 20x, they are quite overvalued for a business that is effectively undifferentiated in the US. A great illustration of this is, if you adjust their gross-profit reporting for this add-back of loss accruals in the US market (their fastest-growing market), the presenter believes they have been making unprofitable loans in order to grow. The presenter thinks next year is going to be a really hard comp for them, because they will be lap ping the “Pay in 8” product launch. They also tend to under-accrue for losses, so you will likely see write-offs ramp as the growth from the previous year flows into write-offs. They also have a large warehouse-debt refinancing in 2027, which the presenter thinks is going to push the issue on the way they are reporting losses.

In terms of a price target, the presenter believes there is 30% to 50% downside.

ideas.th: Hedge against a rate-shock regional-bank break: deposit flight risk amplified by AI cash optimization, at 15x 2027 EPS.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Charles Schwab as a short.

The presenter is pitching Charles Schwab almost as a book hedge, but also due to the rapid rise in yields. Historically, over time, when this has occurred, something in the financial system breaks down. We saw it most recently with the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) in 2023, compounded with the fact that Muse is now being widely adopted by Facebook and by every other LLM.

That creates an opportunity in which you can move from a 0% return on cash balances to 3%-5% if you ask Muse to optimize it. Cash deposits in Schwab have the potential to be at risk, either through yields increasing or Muse doing it for you, as customers look at ways to more efficiently allocate their cash balances.

In 2023, Schwab’s stock fell by ~40% in a matter of weeks after Silicon Valley Bank failed. Bank deposits dropped 11% that quarter, and by the low they were down approximately 35% from the 2022 peak. That move was not caused by anything Schwab did. It was contagion: where investors and clients went looking for the next bank with underwater bonds and cash deposits that could be “at risk”, and Schwab fit that profile. The presenter believes that is the risk here. Schwab will likely have a good quarter when it reports earnings on Thursday, October 15th. But the presenter thinks owning it means you are betting that no other weak link within the regional banking system breaks down, because if one does, Schwab trades down with the group regardless of its own numbers.

In addition, it is not cheap. It is trading at 15x 2027 EPS. The presenter believes that if something like this occurs, Schwab could see ~20% customer deposit withdrawals. Consensus EPS is currently $8 (for 2027). The presenter’s price target is 11x $6, which would equate to a $66 stock price, or 30% downside from current levels.

If nothing breaks and Schwab simply hits consensus, the stock likely has ~20% upside from current levels. And that’s in a tough tape, with AI weighing on the whole group. So, the presenter believes that is the cost of being wrong on this short: approximately 20% if the “stress” event never materializes.

The presenter believes it is a good hedge if things do go wrong. Historically, if interest rates increased by more than 100 bps in a month, something has broken in the regional banking system (in five of the last six occurrences going back to 1974).

ideas.th: Lubricant additives over-earning on old contract wins and price ahead of raws; missile-basket rally overstates AMPAC.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss NewMarket as a short.

NewMarket has an $8 billion cap and $100 million ADV.

The core business is lubricant additives, so it competes with companies such as Lubrizol. Despite its size and liquidity, it has zero sell-side coverage. The stock is up 30% since the beginning of the year and 50% since the start of the Iran war, and it is trading at a peak multiple. There are no estimates, but it is trading at 19x to 20x EPS.

There are two angles to the pitch. One, the core lubricant additive business is 90% of profit and is over-earning. They are benefiting from contracts won two to four years ago, when Lubrizol was capacity-constrained due to its own operational issues. The presenter thinks those contracts are getting re-bid lower. Two, they are benefiting from temporary pricing they took ahead of raw material increases. Their raw materials are petroleum derivatives. In the past, pricing lagged raws. With the Iran war, they went out proactively and took pricing ahead of raws, and that particularly benefited them in Q2. The presenter’s work indicated that they took a bigger increase than competitors, and they are already starting to come down.

Also worth noting, there is Chinese competition from Richful, which is not an issue in the US, but they are gaining share in emerging markets and in some parts of Europe, creating more excess capacity in an industry with flat-to-down volume growth.

As price-cost normalizes and the above-market contracts roll off, gross profit per ton will revert closer to historic levels, which is down 20% from here. Industry volumes are also declining, so time is on your side there.

In terms of the setup, the stock rallied recently on being included in a Citrini basket of beneficiaries from US restocking of missiles. The remaining 10% of operating profit is two-thirds a business called AMPAC, which is one of two providers, the largest, of AP (Ammonium Perchlorate) in the US, the biggest component of solid rocket fuel. So it is true that they benefit from higher US missile procurement, but AP production is used in proportion to the size of the rocket, so they are actually mostly space. The biggest space program is the SLS, which is always at risk of being cancelled. The missiles the US actually needs to buy, like Patriots, do not have much AP in them at all. So, you see these headlines about the US quadrupling (4x) production; in the presenter’s opinion, it is actually a low-single-digit benefit to volumes.

In terms of catalysts, additives is a slow burn. The presenter thinks Q3 is going to be bad in both segments. Part of the reason why the stock was up so much is they had a strong Q2 in both segments. In petroleum additives, they clearly over-earned on price-versus-cost timing. And AMPAC is very volatile quarter to quarter depending on when orders land, and the presenter believes they got all the orders in Q2. So Q3 is going to look bad, and the presenter thinks you have investors who bought this having no idea what it is, because it was included in this basket. The stock is up a lot recently. In Q3 the presenter would look for down 15% to 20%, and then another 15% to 30% as PA (Petroleum Additives) normalizes. The presenter thinks they will earn approximately $40 per share, and at 15x that equates to a $600 to $650 stock price, versus $900 today.

The presenter would like to discuss Cloudflare as a valuation short.

Cloudflare has a $124 billion market cap with only a 2% short interest. The presenter thinks that is the opportunity. The stock is +75% YTD and the presenter thinks investors could make 30% to 40% in terms of the downside.

In the presenter’s opinion, Cloudflare is not a monopoly business the way the market is pricing it. The presenter thinks the reason the sell side likes this stock so much and keeps increasing their price targets is that it used to be a rule-of-40 stock. Then we had whatever happened with Anthropic and Fable, and this panic around security that caused everybody to spend their security budget. So, the presenter thinks there is a lot of pull-forward, and now the company has gone from rule-of-40 to rule-of-50.

If you are the sell-side analyst, your price targets have gone from $280 to $400, using a 43x revenue multiple on next year. The stock is currently trading at 43x this year’s revenue, 33x next year’s revenue, and 26x the year after. Clearly they are going to beat numbers. The presenter thinks the stock could be sub-20x 2028 revenue a year from now. If it is at 26x, investors can make 25% to 30% on the downside.

The bull thesis on the stock has a lot to do with how they play within the agentic backdrop. But part of the challenge is that many of the senior people at this company have actually left, and they have gone to the target customers that you would want. One of the big departures happened a full year ago, and he ended up at Meta. They have lost people to Anthropic. The presenter thinks more high level departures are likely.

A year from now, the company will be facing difficult comps associated with what made the stock such a powerhouse this year (+75% YTD). It is not a complex idea; it is relatively straightforward. It has a 2% short interest. The presenter usually likes to pitch shorts that are more controversial, with 6% to 8% short interest, but they have the potential to squeeze. In this particular case, the presenter believes that you are not going to get squeezed here. It is not Palantir; this company is not changing the planet.

Cloudflare’s CEO loves talking about agentic. He tells you that half the traffic, if not 80% of the traffic, is agentic and bots. He is wrong. If somebody knocks at your front door and you do not let them in, that does not mean it is traffic. There is a lot of inbound bot activity that they block, that Akamai blocks, that everybody blocks, but that does not mean the world has shifted to everything being bot traffic.

The presenter is not saying bot traffic is not the future; it is. But it is not going to be 99% of the traffic—and the presenter thinks if you listen to the company, they would make you believe that is the world we are going into.

ideas.th: Personal-lines agency exposed to agentic AI price shopping, below-industry gross margins and fading contingent commissions at 22x EPS.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Goosehead Insurance as a short.

Goosehead Insurance has a $1.5 billion market cap, ~$2 billion EV, and trades at ~22x EPS. Goosehead is an independent personal-lines insurance agency that operates through its own force of corporate agents, along with a national franchise network.

The presenter likes the setup for the short because of the agentic tools now available to consumers. When Muse came out, they gave an example of trying to save money on insurance. The presenter believes a lot of people have used it, or were trying to use it, to save money on insurance.

Goosehead, instead of buying and rolling up insurance brokers, continues to recruit more agents, so it is growing through broker / headcount growth. Obviously, if there is a big change due to AI and the way business is done in the insurance sector, their business model will be challenged.

Commercial lines are complicated, and it is reasonable to assume brokers that focus on commercial insurance should not be affected. Companies such as Aon, Willis, and Marsh, have been affected, but the presenter would argue that is more sentiment driven. But for Goosehead, while there is a small complication component in home and personal lines, for most of the market it is more traditional cookie-cutter home policies, so the presenter thinks 10% to 20% of commissions are at risk of disintermediation.

But this company is more extreme. It looks like their margins are in line with the industry average, but that is because they show revenues on a net basis, after paying the franchise brokers. If you gross it up, the presenter estimates they actually have below-industry margins. As pricing pressure hits, this company does not have a margin structure where 10% of profits going away is no big deal; they have lower margins than their competitors. In addition, higher interest rates are not great for their business. That is not necessarily a variant perspective, but you are likely not going to get hurt (on the short side) unless there is a major change in rates.

The way the personal-lines industry works is that when there is a lot of profit, the brokers get a cut of it, and when there is no profit, the brokers get less of a cut. It is called contingent payouts. So 2026 is a great year, industry profitability has gotten a lot better, so they have a lot of contingent payouts affecting their EPS. But when pricing is good, more capital flows into the industry, pricing goes down, and the contingent payouts go away. So part of their earnings is more variable than a normal brokerage commission.

The presenter likes that, plus the interest-rate environment affecting mortgage volumes, and on top of that agentic AI creating price competition. It trades at 22x earnings and 15x EBITDA. If agentic AI has any effect on this business, it could have a major impact on earnings and EBITDA.

In the presenter’s view, it seems like an asymmetric risk-reward. The presenter cannot say with confidence that the business is going to fall apart given the agentic AI threat; it could be just the tech-forward people who are using this to save money, and everybody else does not care to adopt. It is hard to know, but the presenter thinks the risk-reward is very attractive. The company has a $150 million buyback, and last quarter they decided not to buy back stock, after buying $30 million to $50 million per quarter. The stock went down after that was announced as well as on the introduction of Muse. It has been going down on housing, pricing in the insurance sector, and the lack of the buyback, but it is still not cheap for an insurance broker.

ideas.th: Rural telco customers squeezed by FWA, Tier-1 fiber and Starlink; organic growth slowing ex-surcharges; EPS 20% below Street.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Calix as a short.

It is a $2.4 billion market cap and $2.2 billion EV equipment vendor to small, Tier 2 and Tier 3 telcos. The stock is currently at $36, trades $40 million per day, and has a 9% short interest. They sell equipment called an optical line terminal, or OLT, which sits in an internet service provider’s central office and routes all the fiber traffic to the homes in the network. They also supply the Wi-Fi routers to each home, and they have an umbrella software offering that lets the provider track its whole network. The equipment stays in service for 10 to 15 years, so the real growth comes from further fiber buildouts, which are mostly saturated in their regions. Within the market there are four key players—Nokia and Cisco at the top, which get pretty much all the business from the large Tier 1 telcos, and then Calix competes with Adtran among the smaller players. Adtran is historically the cheaper option, but Calix has won more business because of its software offering. About three-quarters of Calix’s revenue comes from providers with under 250,000 subs.

The presenter likes the short for four reasons. One, Calix’s small, rural customers are seeing pressure from three fronts. First is fixed wireless access, which is routing your at-home Wi-Fi to a cell tower; Verizon and AT&T added 2 million fixed wireless subs over the last year, approximately 10% of the subscribers in the Tier 3 market.

Second, the Tier 1 fiber buildout is getting more aggressive in the rural areas where Calix’s customers play in. AT&T bought Lumen, and Verizon bought Frontier, which is hurting the smaller players. And Starlink is another headwind. It does not compete on speed compared to fiber, but it is still proving to be a headwind.

Important to note, this year they pushed through surcharges for memory, which has been fueling top-line growth. It has been gross-margin dilutive but gross-profit-dollar neutral, so no real impact to profitability. But their equipment segment growth has decelerated from 36% to 30% to 23% over the last three quarters, and the Q3 guide implies approximately 14% growth. Using the presenter’s math, Q2 organic ex-surcharges would have been less than 20% (around 19%), and Q3 should be around 9%. And you are seeing their customers push back on pricing. If they are not able to keep gross profit dollars neutral, margin could be dilutive and the actual profit dollars could come down.

Three, a big part of the bull case has been BEAD funding, which got delayed but is now rolling out. It is a $20 billion government program to subsidize further fiber buildout. But even if Calix gets the tens of millions they have guided to from this program, it would only contribute low-to-mid-single-digit points of growth over the next few years. It is not material in the presenter’s opinion.

Finally, their software business (which management has historically promoted which has led the stock to trade at a premium to Adtran), the presenter believes they are still being promotional, but it is still less than 20% of revenue. They created some agentic AI solutions, but the presenter believes that not many people will be using an agent to track their fiber usage. The Street has that growth accelerating from high teens this year to mid-20%s, and the presenter thinks that will be pressured.

Putting it all together, the stock is currently trading at 21x 2026 EPS and 16x 2027 EPS. The presenter gets to $1.80 of EPS in 2027, approximately 20% below the Street, driven by software growth decelerating to mid-teens rather than mid-20%s, and equipment revenue decelerating to high single digits rather than low double digits. Putting a 15x multiple on that, a one-turn discount to next year’s multiple, gets you a $27 stock, or 25% downside from current levels.

ideas.th: Roll-up whose growth is bought, not built: organic growth turning negative, NRR below 100%, 2.4x levered, with lockup expiry ahead.
ideas.cat: Lockup expiry 48 hours after Q3 earnings in November
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Bending Spoons as a short.

There seem to be some investors who like to discuss Muse losers, but if you like tech Muse losers, you can get them all here.

For background, Bending Spoons is a serial acquirer of orphaned consumer internet companies. They acquire companies like AOL, Vimeo, WeTransfer, Eventbrite, and Tractive, at low multiples—2x to 3x sales—and wrap them into their internal earnings-generation engine. In the presenter’s opinion, their team of what they call “Spooners” takes these assets, applies some AI capabilities, expands margins, cuts some of the internal staff, and then raises price 100% + on the existing customer base. So what you have is a roll-up where all of the growth is bought and not built.

They IPO’d earlier this summer. FY2025 organic growth was +12%, Q1 2026 was +6%, Q2 2026 was +3%, and they are now lapping tougher comps from recent acquisitions, including Tractive, a pet-tracking-device company, in Q3. So they will likely have negative organic growth in Q3. Despite the price increases they took (there are examples on Twitter of customers opening their Vimeo accounts and seeing a 400% price increase overnight), they are still below 100% NRR. The presenter thinks that ends up closer to 90% to 95% in Q3. The presenter believes that all the value comes from taking price and cutting the existing R&D and S&M teams, which is a great setup for a Muse loser, even if you think this engine was sustainable before Muse.

In terms of M&A, they have done $7 billion of acquisitions in TEV since inception. Approximately half of that has been done YTD. The presenter believes that much of the growth engine and their ability to raise prices on customers, while also reducing cost is untested here. The management team is well regarded, but this is their first experience running a public company (the co-CFOs and the CEO), and, in the presenter’s opinion, now they are managing a business with sub-100% NRR and 2.4x leverage.

The opportunity here is that the lockup on existing shareholders ends 48 hours after Q3 earnings in November. Before then, the presenter acknowledges that there is a lot of danger being short the shares. Just two weeks ago, the presenter thinks there was short covering that took the share price up ~25% in a single session. But if you can get comfortable after the lockup expires, there is a real opportunity for a re-rate. In the presenter’s opinion, investors are buying companies at 2x to 3x sales that get marked up to 6x sales immediately, despite the fundamentals and net revenue retention weakening.

Approximately 70% of free cash flow is generated almost entirely by AOL, so you are almost buying AOL here. That acquisition was completed approximately six months ago. They teased the idea of raising prices on their last earnings call, and that could really be playing with fire. The presenter thinks there is an asymmetric risk/reward opportunity once the lockup expires.

Bio-Rad is made up of two components. First, they own a significant stake in Sartorius, a European bioprocessing company, which the presenter thinks is a long. They also have a core business, which is a diagnostics / life-sciences-related business. The stub trades at ~10x 2027 core EBITDA once you back out the Sartorius stake, and the presenter thinks there is a reasonable chance that Street numbers for 2027 for Bio-Rad core are too high. If you go back to 2018, core Bio-Rad has only grown top line at a 2% organic revenue CAGR, over a period when inflation was likely +3.5%. It is kind of a shrinker over time.

In terms of the math, if the stock trades down to 7x or 8x 2027 EBITDA on a core basis, and you hold Sartorius at the current market value, the whole package trades from $370 today to approximately $300 on 2027 numbers. ideas.th: Indeed's 35% listing price hikes are one-time as AI hiring tools commoditize; FX tailwind fades and AI-loser re-rating risk.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Recruit Holdings as a short.

Recruit has a $154 billion enterprise value and a $160 billion market cap. Approximately 45% of revenues and three-quarters of EBITDA this year come from what they call “HR technology.” That is primarily Indeed.com, and to a lesser extent Glassdoor. HR technology revenues are 80% US and international (Europe), and 20% Japan. Another 45% of revenues and 10% of EBITDA come from the staffing business, split 50/50 between Japan and the rest of the world, and the balance is a small marketing and booking business in Japan. So economically, three-quarters of this business is Indeed.com and Glassdoor, tilted to the US. Indeed.com is a job board that acts as a “top of funnel” for companies collecting resumes from prospective job applicants. Companies pay to list their jobs on the platform (a paid-listings model), and to a much lesser extent, pay for additional services from Indeed.com like processing those resumes.

In terms of the setup, Recruit’s stock is +100% YTD because Recruit has meaningfully raised what it charges for those job listings (i.e. if you are Amazon or Walmart or an SMB, what they charge you to advertise your job to a prospective candidate). They have raised the revenue per job listing by 35% year-year in dollar terms. They have done this by introducing new higher tiers of premium paid listings and eliminating many of the free tiers people were using. Recruit says its new premium listings give SMBs AI tools to sort through resumes and schedule interviews, which is allowing it to take price.

The presenter acknowledges that they do not have a smoking gun, but they think the risk-reward is compelling for a few reasons. First, fundamentally, the presenter views the price increases as one-time in nature as they start to roll through. Recruit introduced these AI features, such as resume sorting and scheduling, a little ahead of the curve, but they are ChatGPT-backed—that is the engine that powers them—and they are being rapidly rolled out by HR systems of record and new AI upstarts, such as Juicebox and Gem, for a cheap price or free. The presenter sees more limited scope for price increases moving forward, as these capabilities have already become commoditized at this point.

Second, while a lot of the profit growth year over year is organic pricing, there is also an FX tailwind this year, because a lot of the revenues are derived overseas, while the expense base is largely in yen, and there has been a lot of dollar and euro strength.

Third, the valuation does not look demanding for a category killer (if you think Indeed.com is the dominant job-listing platform). The company trades at 25x 2026 EBIT (using the presenter’s estimates), but half the revenues come from lower-margin, no-growth businesses. So the market is putting $135 billion of value on $9 billion of Indeed.com and Glassdoor revenues outside of Japan. That equates to ~13x revenue and a much higher EBITDA multiple (something in the 30s).

Fourth, it is unclear to the presenter that Indeed.com is actually a long-term AI winner. They have been able to raise prices and execute somewhat better than other job boards in the near term. But if you look at competitors like ZipRecruiter or Seek (a publicly traded Australian job board), the presenter does not think their businesses are differentiated, and those stocks are down 60% to 70% from a few years ago. They have been put in the AI-loser bucket, while Indeed.com is currently in the AI-winner bucket. The presenter does not think it takes much for investors to question why AI shouldn’t lower the barriers for applicants to apply directly to jobs, and for companies to screen and filter candidates without a job board or a third party?

The presenter conservatively sees 25% downside from current levels, valuing the US and international HR tech business at 15x EBITDA, and that assumes Recruit continues to take a lot of price. The presenter sees meaningful further downside if market perception changes and this gets put into the AI-loser bucket.

ideas.th: Synthetic-to-natural color shift (MAHA, Walmart) turns $100M into ~$1B revenue; $7-8 2028 EPS vs low-$6 Street.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Sensient Technologies as a long.

Sensient has a $5.5 billion market cap / $6.3 billion EV. It is currently levered 2.8x, but they will be de-levering rather quickly due to a peaking investment cycle. For context, it trades at ~20x 2028 consensus earnings of $6.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes the story is underfollowed / under-the-radar. Roughly a third of EBIT is derived from flavors and extracts. It is essentially a specialty chemical company, with flavors and extracts selling to food, beverage, pharmaceutical, and personal care companies. They generally sell to small to midsize CPG, so they are selling to smaller, upstart, growing businesses, which is why their business is growing mid-single digits, with high-teens EBITDA margins. The company thinks they can get that to the low-to-mid 20%s over time.

The crux of the thesis is that they sell color into companies as an ingredient. That is approximately half of the EBIT, and the crux of the thesis. They produce both natural and synthetic colors in foods, beverages, pharmaceuticals, personal care, etc. They sell that to both large and small companies. There has been a large push, which was started by the MAHA (Make American Healthy Again) movement, moving away from synthetic dyes to using only natural colors. It started as a voluntary pledge by the industry, but it is more commercial and societal pressure that is driving the change now.

They have $100 million of synthetic color revenue in the US that they think will convert to $1 billion dollars of revenue over the next several years. The reason why there is that uplift is that if you take Red 40, and you want to make a Skittle that is red, they know it is one part. In order to do that with natural colors, you need to use beets, carrots, and other natural ingredients from the ground – so it is more volume and at higher prices.

They are one of the only companies, possibly in the world, but definitely in the US, that can do this. There are other companies that do it, but do not have the same breadth of offerings. Some of them only have certain color offerings. What is unique about Sensient is that they are already working with all of these companies, and they are assisting them with the transition. So they are in a pole position to win.

We are kind of in the bottom of the first inning. The presenter would say the transition is being triggered by, at the start of 2027, Walmart says that all of their own private label needs to be (or will be) natural colors. All new products going into Walmart need to be natural colors. Target, all cereals in their stores today are natural colors. There is other state legislature for K-12 schools and others that starts in 2028, so there is a massive push there. What is interesting is that it is kind of difficult to do this from a supply-chain perspective, both on the Sensient side (and why they are well ahead from a CAPEX and working-capital perspective) but also from the company perspective. To say you are only going to do it for K-12 is really difficult to do from an R&D, supply chain, and manufacturing process perspective. The presenter has done a lot of work on this, and when you speak to large CPG companies, they are essentially doing all of this at the same time.

In the third quarter of 2025, they invoiced $1 million of this $1 billion. Then it went to $5 million, then it went to approximately $10 and $15 million. So, the company has invoiced $45 million of the $1 billion opportunity. That should accelerate in the back half of this year, and then again through 2027.

At this early stage, the presenter believes that they have both the supply chain and the technical skills to achieve this, by working alongside the likes of General Mills, Campbells, Nestlé, and Conagra. And they front-loaded many of the OPEX investments. The CAPEX and working-capital investments will be over a couple of years. But from here, incremental margins should be a lot better than what we have seen to date.

And the fieldwork has come back so universally positive that this is not going backwards. Things could change quarter to quarter, but it is universally positive that Sensient is in pole position to win. Guidance feels like it is in a good place. The presenter thinks management likes to be conservative. They feel like they have better visibility on the top line than the middle of the P&L, only because there are investments that they are making. But to date, they have beaten expectations.

The presenter thinks we see continued quarter-over-quarter growth in the conversion from synthetic to natural. The presenter thinks earnings power is $7 to $8 in 2028, versus the Street at low $6s. The presenter thinks there is still an opportunity to compound from there. They have said, at a recent conference, they think they can get to a $1 billion run-rate in the first half of 2028 (that would be upside to the presenter's numbers).

If you think about this business relative to Givaudan, Symrise, or IFF - if you roll forward what this is going to look like from 2026 to 2028 and then some, it is going to have faster revenue growth, faster EBITDA growth, faster earnings growth, and margins that are very similar to those peers that are trading at 25x. And they will still be in the early-to-mid innings, because there is still an opportunity in the US, still opportunity in personal care, makeup and cosmetics, as well as in pet.

The stock is currently trading at ~$130. The presenter thinks it could easily be a $175 to $200 stock as we exit next year and investors think about what the earnings power could be in 2028, which will continue to ramp. It is also not out of the realm of possibility that it could be acquired.

ideas.th: Cleaned-up oligopoly residential products at ~8x EBITDA vs 10-13x private-market comps; deleveraging plus SOTP/take-private angle.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Resideo as a long.

Resideo is a residential products company. The stock currently trades at $18 per share and the presenter thinks it could be worth over $30.

It is a residential products company mostly exposed to oligopoly markets, with 40%-plus gross margin, 20%-plus EBITDA margin, with 3% to 5% top-line growth. It is trading in the low 8x on 2026 EBITDA and low 9x EBITDA minus CAPEX.

In terms of the business, 30% is air, which is thermostats / indoor air quality with approximately 50% market share in this segment. 23% is safety, which consists of fire alarms, CO2 alarms, fire suppression with approximately 50% market share in this segment. 20% is global climate solutions, which are products for boilers, water heaters, furnaces, and heat pumps. 16% is security, which is intrusion panels, sensors, and cameras. 11% is water, which is valves and heads for water control, plumbing, and heating.

For context, the private equity bid for each of these businesses is between 10x to 12x, and we have seen a number of recent acquisitions in the space. Lone Star bought Kidde, which is the other oligopolistic player in the fire alarm market, for a bit north of 10x, and the presenter believes they are eventually going to look to IPO somewhere in the double digits to low teens (which might be hard, given that their closest comp is trading at 8x). Reliance Worldwide is a company that is getting taken out by Brookfield for just shy of 13x. Emerson carved out Copeland and sold it to Blackstone for mid-12x.

The presenter thinks there is an earnings improvement story here, a rebuilding-credibility story, and it can re-rate and grow by itself. However, the presenter thinks there is an interesting activist or take-private, sum-of-the-parts story as well. The story in the past has been very difficult to invest in, and they have cleaned it up a lot. They used to pay out $140 million per year due to a Honeywell environmental liability. After they spun out from Honeywell, that is now gone. They spun out a more volatile piece of their business in ADI Global Distribution, which increased earnings volatility and dragged down the organic growth of the business. That is now out. It is a touch levered, at 3.2x net debt, but the presenter thinks they can de-lever to 2x by mid-2028 and start buying back stock. Then with execution (the presenter is in line to slightly above Street numbers), they think the stock can re-rate from here.

Post-Investor Day, in the first-quarter reporting as a standalone company, there were a couple of very minor headwinds, about 5% on second-half EBITDA, that hurt their credibility / poor communication which ultimately dragged down the stock. But the presenter thinks those factors will be proof that in the next couple of quarters as being not too much of an issue, while the earnings growth formula is still intact.

ideas.th: Nascent space, missile and marine defense lines plus OEM LTA repricing drive 20%+ EPS growth vs mid-teens Street.
ideas.cat: OEM LTA repricing over next 6-12 months
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss RBC Bearings as a long.

The market cap is $16 billion. They are a manufacturer of highly engineered precision bearings, motion control products, and valves. For reference, 55% of their revenue is tied to industrial end markets and approximately 45% is tied to aerospace and defense (as well as a space business).

What separates this company from other bearings manufacturers like Timken or Regal is that they focus on highly specialized pieces, which get co-designed with their customers early in the design phase, and get spec'd into long-duration programs, which lends itself to attractive pricing power and economics relative to these other players. So they have compounded earnings at a much higher rate than peers over the last 20 years; so, structurally it is a very good business.

There are three key factors as to why the presenter thinks it is interesting today. One, within the industrial business, you are seeing this ongoing positive inflection in short-cycle industrials, which the presenter thinks will accelerate their organic growth to high singles to low doubles over the next few quarters, which is slightly above where the Street is. But the most interesting piece of the business is in the aerospace and defense segment, where you have three new growing businesses - space, missile, and marine defense. Collectively, these businesses are a low double-digit percent of total revenue and very difficult to model because they are so nascent; as a result, the presenter believes investors will not find them in any sell-side models. But there is very good demand visibility over the next few years to potentially doubling or tripling these businesses in the medium term. The presenter thinks that presents a pretty attractive upside toggle that is not priced into industry estimates. That is really interesting on top line.

And then on margins, you have this attractive story where, over the next 6 to 12 months, approximately 40% of their commercial OEM LTAs are getting repriced, and in some cases by as much as 35% to 40% in terms of step-ups. If you put these pieces together, the presenter thinks the business should be growing earnings over 20% over the next three years, versus the Street that is only assuming mid-teens growth.

In summary, the presenter believes this is a really interesting setup where you have a great business with multiple ways to win, and with the pullback in A&D multiples recently, you have a more attractive, reasonable entry point today.

The presenter models ~30% upside over the next 12 months. The thinking there is, the presenter is high single digits above the Street on earnings, and then you assume the multiple remains flat from here.

ideas.th: Virtual used-car auction growing EBITDA to $500M by 2028; ACV sale to Copart at 15x makes OpenLane a strategic target.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss OpenLane as a long.

OpenLane has a $4 billion (unlevered) EV.

OpenLane operates a virtual used car auction.

The simple way to think about the company is, they generated $300 million of EBITDA last year going to $500 million in 2028. They are a beneficiary of declining used car pricing and a beneficiary of virtual auctions taking share from physical auctions. The timely piece of news is that a much smaller competitor of theirs, ACV, based up in Rochester, was recently bought for $2 billion or 15x EBITDA, by Copart.

There is a long entanglement of companies here. For context, OpenLane used to be KAR Auction Services. They sold their physical auction business to Carvana. Ritchie Brothers is a competitor to Copart. They might view virtual auctions as something they might need to get into, and the presenter thinks OpenLane would be an obvious strategic target for them. The company did a secondary and a co-lead investor, a private equity firm, sold stock. The stock took a hit and never really recovered. The company bought back stock in the deal. The CEO bought stock in the open market after. Roughly, call it $400 million of EBITDA, $250 million of free cash flow, and 100% of free cash flow to buy back stock. The presenter thinks it is a clean / simple story where you do not have to think about AI. The presenter’s price target is $60, or 15x $500 million, and then investors can discount that back however you would like.

ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss MasTec as a long.

MasTech has a market cap of $16 billion, with $4.2 billion in debt, generating approximately $500 million of free cash flow per year and growing.

In terms of the setup, the stock is down ~60% in the last two to three months. The pitch is simple, this is a business that is going to grow. The top line is compounding at 15%+ plus deals with leverage to the bottom line. In the presenter’s opinion, there were a lot of generalist investors in the E&C space and they seem to have all exited the stock. You now have a business that is trading around 8x 2028 EBITDA, which is back to the pre-AI low end of the EBITDA range.

Why did the stock sell off so much? The presenter would say, if you benchmark MasTec to best in breed, which is Quanta - Quanta is down approximately 30% from its peak - that is the industry component of the sell off. The idiosyncratic part is they have two businesses. One is 15% of the top line and 14% of EBITDA in communications, where half is wireless, half is wireline where they had a slight pushout of a project. The presenter would simply say that the communications segment is not the most exciting part of the story, while the balance of the business (80%+) is far more interesting. The presenter thinks the communications business is fine where it is, with 8% margins, but the presenter is not underwriting that getting materially better.

The presenter will lead with why the business is growing so much. It is simply the dynamic with utilities, where utilities have had flat budgets. Utilities give you 10-year capital plans. They have been flat for 20+ years. They inflected two years ago. They will be growing for the next eight to ten years based on their 10-year forecasts, and MasTec is tied to that, as is Quanta and others.

The 80%+ of sales and EBITDA that are tied to that, should double from last year through 2028, compounding organically 15% +, in addition to the acquisitions that they are making as they de-lever.

The presenter does not think that they have a large EBITDA discrepancy versus the Street, but they would argue that you have had a material de-rating to the tune of 60%, and the presenter thinks you are now back to the low end of the EBITDA range for a business that legitimately grows. Effectively, nothing has changed in terms of the risk profile of the business. In the presenter’s opinion, there were a lot of investors in the stock that did not appreciate the dynamics and volatility of an engineering company.

ideas.th: AI-driven drug discovery accelerates LC/mass-spec spend, lifting IDEX's HST mass-spec business toward low-double-digit growth.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss IDEX Corporation as a long.

IDEX is an industrial conglomerate with a $17 billion market cap, levered at a little less than 1x based on the presenter's numbers.

The presenter thinks the part of the story that is well understood is that they have a lot of short-cycle industrial businesses, plus a semis business, in addition to a Bloom Energy tie-up from their core power business. The additional upside now is what is happening in the biopharma markets - particularly with the life science tools companies like Agilent, Waters, Danaher, and Thermo Fisher. They have basically been on the road for two straight months telling you that there is a real tailwind to their businesses, particularly on the liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry cycle, because AI infrastructure integrated into drug discovery labs, particularly wet labs, is actually driving an incremental pickup in the amount of drug discovery processes that they can run.

Consequently, what is happening is that there is a major tug on an already inflecting liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry equipment spending cycle, and that is accelerating the fundamentals for all of these companies. You can see it in the commentary from Agilent and Waters. You can see it from the underlying tone of the companies, as well as their stock price reactions.

Why this matters for IDEX is that they have a large mass spectrometry business that comprises a meaningful percentage of their HST business. If that inflects meaningfully, it layers on top of a pre-existing bull thesis. The presenter thinks the bulls underwrite an acceleration of 5% to 6% organic growth to approximately 8% next year. Layering this on top of that could yield closer to low double digits growth.

IDEX has commanded a high 20s multiple in terms of its P/E multiple historically. If it gets to high 20s on the presenter's numbers, that would equate to 30% upside by year end when this all gets realized. In the presenter’s opinion, this creates a positive tug on the backlog as well, which the company clearly trades on going into year end.
