ideas.th: New ex-DHL CEO shifting to higher-value contracts; backlog inflecting and Q3/Analyst Day can re-rate 12x P/E toward 20-30x.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss GXO as a long.

GXO is an outsourced contract warehouse and logistics operator (it spun out of XPO pre-COVID). The pandemic was the mother of all booms for outsourcing warehousing, as everyone needed to build inventories because the supply chain was so broken. Their business boomed. A lot of contracts were signed. And given that they have a fair amount of exposure to Europe, that bust has been extremely painful, but the presenter thinks we are finally through the worst of it.

The bust was exacerbated by a few management mistakes. First, they got hurt by an acquisition that they made in Europe which froze their sales force. Second, they bid on low-risk contracts, mostly in Europe, where it is a more competitive market.

Important to note, this is a greenfield opportunity with only 20% to 30% of Europe being outsourced. In the US, it is closer to 10% to 15%, so there is an enormous greenfield opportunity, and the cost curve has steepened with material growth ahead.

In terms of the management team, they fired their CEO, and subsequently brought in the head of DHL Logistics, who the presenter thinks is considered a superstar. He has been in the position for approximately one year but investors are growing impatient because it takes a little while to turn the Titanic. He is focusing on higher-margin, stickier business where they can add more value. Think of it as the following - if Kohl's only has eight pairs of size 10 shoes on the store floor, it is a problem. If the Boeing actuator does not show up to the plant for just-in-time inventory, it is an existential problem. So they are moving into higher-value-add aerospace, biotech, AI data center management, etc.

Investors have been waiting for this backlog to materialize but the presenter acknowledges that it does take time. This past quarter, the actual backlog and billings booked really inflected. The CEO is out there insisting that this trend is accelerating. However, their organic growth slipped to 3.5% from the guided 4% to 5%. The presenter thinks you have long-only accounts (back from the pandemic days) that are fed up. You have investors that follow the CEO that are losing confidence, because this is taking a bit more time. And then you have all the passive investors in industrials that likely got out as well (fears around diesel, etc.).

The presenter strongly suspects that a contract had slipped, which indicates to the presenter that the third quarter should be strong. The presenter believes that the CEO sounds really confident about the quarter. Important to note, they have an Analyst Day after this quarter. Should this trajectory on new wins continue and they start to print 6%, 7%, or 8% organic growth, the presenter believes this goes from 12x P/E today and 7x EBITDA to 14x to 18x EBITDA and 20x to 30x P/E very quickly, as the compound story here is very powerful.

ideas.th: Amazon deal marks the peak: Caterpillar/Cummins capacity, Amazon control and Chinese engine risk compress the 16x P/E to 12x.

The presenter would like to discuss Generac as a short.

Generac is the marginal provider of power equipment for backup for data centers. Two weeks ago, they announced a monster deal with Amazon: $2.4 billion over the next two years and $8 billion through 2030. Amazon gets 2% of the business for that.

The presenter thinks this deal is going to be the last one they announce, because they think there are three factors that will work against the company. Even if they do not, the presenter thinks the price for these gensets is only going to go one direction, particularly if the Chinese start getting more deals.

The presenter thinks it is worth 35% less than it is currently, using a 12x multiple instead of 16x consensus. As soon as investors see that capacity come online for the other players, the multiple compresses.

ideas.th: Price actions recover ~$800M of price-cost not in consensus as inflation laps; $18 2027 EPS vs Street below $16.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Eaton as a long.

The presenter believes there are really two drivers to the thesis. The first is price-cost and margins, and the second is just organic growth. On the price-cost side, if you look at Electrical Americas (EA), wage and commodity inflation have been a 450 to 500-basis point margin headwind in that segment for each of the last four quarters, and roughly 80% of that is commodity inflation.

During the CFO transition last fall (in November), their price-cost simply got away from them during that period of time. The presenter thinks it was, on a dollar basis, in EA roughly a $300 million headwind in the first half, and on a gross dollar basis, something like $600 million in EA for the year when you roll through commodity pricing through the back half. The new CFO started in early March, and he has made it a clear priority to be recouping that. So they took price in April, they took price again in August, and they have stated that they intend to be dollar-neutral on a full-year basis, with more price earning in Q4 relative to Q3. Investors can do that math in terms of dollars that they are going to get. The presenter thinks they put some of this - but not all of it - in their second-half margin bridge. Then you have a similar dynamic, but on a smaller scale, playing out in EG as well. Where the presenter thinks it looks interesting is into 2027, where inflation will start to lap, but you will get the full-year benefit of the pricing actions. The presenter thinks that is not modeled in consensus. The presenter thinks the clearest way to see that is in incremental margins, where at their investor event in 2025, they guided to a framework for the combined global electrical business that implied a 35% incremental margin (2030 over 2024 as your base year). When you look at consensus for 2027 over 2024 (2024 is a clean base, and 2027 would be the year that you fully lap the price-cost headwinds) consensus has a 27% incremental margin. So the dollar basis there between the 27% incremental and the 35% incremental is about $800 million. The presenter thinks that is $800 million effectively of price that is unrecouped in consensus numbers. So the Street is modeling the headwind going away but does not incorporate the price impact on earnings. That is the thesis as it relates to margins. If you zoom out, Eaton is in a position where the two pain points in industrials (either price-cost or manufacturing ramps), are accelerating out the other end of the tunnel on both of those as you go into next year. Then the second piece is on organic growth, where they have been chasing numbers up all year. They are implying in their guidance a deceleration in the second half in both EA and EG. The presenter thinks they are likely to beat that. If you put everything together - margins and organic growth - looking to next year consensus is less than $16 EPS while the presenter thinks they can earn $18 EPS. If you hold the current multiple, roll that forward on $18 next year, it would equate to a $525 stock price.

ideas.th: Backlog doubled to $1.6B riding the gas-turbine cycle a year behind GE Vernova; Street revenue too low for an under-covered name.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss CECO Environmental as a long.

It has a $4 billion market cap, levered 2.5x, and trades approximately $50 to 60 million per day.

The story here is that they did a transformative acquisition six months ago. They bought a company called Thermon, which focuses on heat tracing (cables and wires). The presenter believes standalone CECO is very interesting, but investors were questioning why they were doing this deal.

The core business has doubled backlog from $800 million to $1.6 billion in the last two quarters, because they are essentially a year behind GE Vernova and Siemens in terms of the power generation cycle. They sell scrubbers, products that reduce noise and reduce emissions. They have 70% market share for their products on turbines 200 megawatts and up. The presenter thinks their content per megawatt can grow substantially. The presenter believes that they are a year behind GE Vernova and Siemens in the order cycle. All the big orders that those companies started to book two years ago, CECO is starting to see that now. According to a sell-side note, the big project they just won is $350 million of content on Project Kilby, the big data center in Texas with Microsoft and Chevron.

The story here is that the backlog has doubled and they are now seeing good operating leverage. They are mostly contract manufactured, so they do not have to add all this capacity to capitalize on this demand. They can simply serve the orders when they get them. The presenter thinks they can generate $2 billion of revenue next year while the Street is at $1.8 billion. This year they are likely going to book $3 billion of orders. If you think about how these turbine orders have occurred over the last two years, they likely book another $3 billion next year. They are going to exit 2027 with $3 billion of backlog and potentially $3 billion of revenue. Typically they convert backlog over 12 to 18 months.

The presenter believes it is a situation where Street numbers are materially too low. It is not a well-trafficked company as it is only covered by approximately five analysts. A new sell-side analyst just picked up coverage two months ago, and it has started to generate more buzz / attention. But the presenter thinks the story is that power generation is 30% of revenue and will be growing to 50% or 60% over the next two years. They also have a lot of exposure to gas pipeline and midstream; that is another 20%. The rest is a mix of other oil & gas markets and general industrial. They have some semiconductor manufacturing exposure as well. The non-power-gen business is mostly focused on filtration and dust collection. These are sleepy industrial businesses but the presenter thinks the entire company can grow 20% to 30% organic for the next four years.

Based on the presenter's numbers, the stock trades at ~12x 2027 EBITDA. The presenter thinks there is a meaningful discovery-value situation occurring, where investors are figuring out that this company / opportunity exists, and numbers should go materially higher. Obviously, there is an AI angle to the story as well. Investors want to say that we are at peak gas turbine orders, but because of the timing of when CECO books orders, the presenter does not think you are going to see that peak until 2028 or maybe even into 2029. In summary, it is an undiscovered story with material numbers upside. The company does a lot of marketing. They were at Laguna, and they were at a sell-side conference. They are trying to get more sell-side coverage. EBITDA margins are going from 10% to 20% over the next three years. And as it relates to Thermon, they share a lot of the same end markets, and they have a lot of the same customers. So, there are a lot of cross-selling opportunities that are already being booked. In the presenter’s opinion, it is not in the deal assumptions. They are already tracking ahead on the cost synergies. The presenter thinks the earnings power of the combined business is materially higher.

ideas.th: Cement maker at 4.3x EBITDA with €900M net cash; US pricing and EU carbon fears overdone, history of step-up EBITDA.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Buzzi as a long.

It is a €37 stock, €6.7 billion market cap. There is €900 million of net cash, and they also own a third of a Mexican cement company called Moctezuma that is worth €1.2 billion. The EV is approximately €4.8 billion. The stock is very cheap. It trades at 4.3x EBITDA and 7x P/E ex cash. The JV income from Mexico sits below the EBITDA line.

The stock is down ~30% year to date on concerns regarding pricing power in the US cement market and European regulatory dynamics coming into focus once again. The company is largely a cement supplier with some concrete and aggregates exposure. For context, 40% to 50% of their EBITDA is in the US, approximately 10% is in Brazil, and then 40% to 50% is in Europe.

In the US, cement prices have been flat to down 1% year to date, which is causing margin pressure across the industry, given rising input costs, particularly diesel. At the same time, demand has been weak, as construction markets remain soft. The weak pricing backdrop, especially in the face of higher energy costs, is driving the narrative that the cement industry pushed too much pricing during the 2022 to 2024 time frame. There is also heightened competition from imports, which the presenter does not believe to be the primary driver. Imports as a share of total industry volumes rose from 2013 to 2022, but they have stagnated since 2022 to roughly 20% to 21% share. The presenter thinks weak pricing is more a function of volume declines and they expect better price realization and cost recovery in 2027. Outside the US, the competitive dynamics are better. The company reported slight EBITDA growth ex-US in the first half, despite all of the energy pressures. But there is renewed investor focus on the EU's planned phase-out of free carbon credits to the cement industry over the next decade, which will gradually increase the fee paid per ton of cement produced. Bearish investors think Buzzi is in a worse position than peers, because they have not been as quick to spend capital on decarbonization projects or carbon capture plants. The presenter thinks Buzzi is simply taking a different approach, where they are not committing significant capital before it is clear how the economics will play out. Given this is an industry-wide issue, the presenter sees cement pricing across Europe increasing in response to higher environmental costs, which is similar to what happened during the energy crisis following the Ukraine war.

Stepping back, there is a lot of focus on year-to-date profitability, but this is a business that has dramatically increased profitability and improved its balance sheet over time. If you look at historical results, you can see that EBITDA consolidates around a certain level for a few years and then increases significantly. From 2016 to 2018, EBITDA was in the €500 to €600 million range. Then from 2019 to 2021, it was in the €700 to €800 million range. The company has been in the €1.15 to €1.25 billion range since 2023. At the same time, the business used to have over one turn of leverage, but they have generated a lot of free cash flow and now sit with €900 million of net cash, which they can use for acquisitions and share buybacks. The presenter thinks just showing some level of EBITDA growth from here can drive a significant re-rating. Looking out to 2028, if the presenter puts 7x on €1.25 billion of EBITDA - which is approximately 11x P/E ex-cash - and a 6% free cash flow yield - the stock would be worth €61, or over 60% upside. It is worth noting that in the presenter's price target, it excludes the Russia business, which likely has no value following the fallout from the Ukraine war.

ideas.th: Under-levered, asset-rich airline oligopoly buying back stock; Aeroplan marked at ~$10B vs $13B EV, on path to double.
ideas.cat: Possible new normal course issuer bid in November
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Air Canada as a long.

Air Canada has a $12.5 billion EV, $6.6 billion market cap, and a little less than $6 billion net debt including leases. It trades over $75 million per day. It is the number one Canadian airline, with over 40% domestic market share. The top two players have over 70% share, so it is a true oligopoly, but with a better structure compared to the US market.

Aside from the top two players, every single other airline in Canada took money from the Canadian government because of fuel prices. The only two players that did not were WestJet and Air Canada, and they are the only ones that can make the business work. It is a different form of what happened in the US, with the low-cost carriers going bankrupt (i.e. Spirit). This is very different from the pandemic, when the Canadian government forced every airline to issue shares. Air Canada took part in that during the pandemic, where they issued shares. Prior to that, there were ten years where the share count had not moved. Now, since Q4 2024, they have retired a third of the shares outstanding. They issued a normal course issuer bid in the fourth quarter of 2024, and bought back 10% of their stock. They settled some converts in May of 2025. They did another normal course issuer bid.

Recently, they closed on a 10% share buyback of the company, but they still have a lot of cash on the balance sheet. Over 100% of market cap is in cash, and they are less than two turns net levered. The presenter thinks they will potentially do another normal course issuer bid for another 10% in November. So they are massively under-levered, they are asset rich, they own over 80% of their fleet, and they have agreements to sell $2 billion of their fleet over the next 18 months - again, versus a sub-$7 billion market cap.

The most recent / interesting component to the story - they own Aeroplan, which is the largest loyalty program in Canada. They sold a 25% stake to Blackstone and a consortium for a $10 billion implied value. They are able to buy back that 25% stake at a 6.5% IRR to Blackstone. The value of Aeroplan is being marked by private equity at $10 billion against a $13 billion EV. They also have pension assets - net surplus funding that is $4 billion or so - and then the actual planes that they own, which the presenter estimates are worth over $10 billion in terms of book value.

Worth noting, last year WestJet received an investment from Delta and others that valued the company at 6x EBITDA, which is higher than where United trades currently. In 2024, Air Canada put out a plan to generate $5 billion of EBITDA by 2028. The Iran war obviously throws a wrinkle into that most likely, but even if they generate $4 billion or so, which is conservative, the presenter thinks the stock is on a path to doubling over the next 18 months.

ideas.th: European alarm leader at ~10% steady-state FCF yield; heavy reinvestment masks cash flow and AI/PE-overhang fears are misplaced.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Verisure as a long.

Verisure is the number one professionally monitored alarm provider in Europe and LATAM, selling and installing proprietary hardware, and generating revenue through monthly monitoring fees. It has a €9 billion market cap and a €14 billion EV. It IPO'd in October 2025. This is a high-quality compounder trading at a 10% steady-state free cash flow yield and approximately 6x steady-state EBITDA, that is misunderstood by the market for a few reasons. One, there are significant reinvestments masking cash flow potential. Two, there is a misunderstood AI risk. And three, there is a PE sponsor overhang.

With more than 6 million subscribers, the company has nearly 40% share of the installed base across its footprint. However, its footprint is just 4% penetrated, while the US market has a penetration of over 20%. In order to capture this massive TAM, Verisure is currently reinvesting approximately 70% of its steady-state free cash flow into acquiring new customers. Investors seem to struggle to understand how attractive this reinvestment opportunity is. With leading 7% attrition rates and impressive margins, the presenter thinks Verisure is generating 20% unlevered IRRs on each new customer, supporting double-digit free cash flow growth for years to come.

There are concerns that AI-enabled tech poses a threat to Verisure. The presenter does not think this view really holds water. The company has continued to grow uninterrupted for decades, despite concerns that DIY offerings from tech giants like Amazon and Google would take share. Moreover, in many of its core markets, regulations require alarm systems to be professionally installed and monitored, creating a meaningful barrier to entry for new competitors lacking Verisure's 12,000-person sales and installation workforce. Rather than being disrupted by AI, the presenter expects Verisure to benefit from the implementation of AI, improving efficiency across all aspects of its business.

As it relates to the PE sponsor overhang, the company was IPO'd in October 2025 by Hellman and Friedman (H&F), who have owned this company since 2011. To extend the life of the investment, H&F completed a fund transfer of the asset in December 2020 after realizing an 8x MOIC on its initial investment. The presenter believes that H&F are likely true long-term believers in Verisure's potential and have a history of holding assets for 20+ years. With today's share price at nearly the new fund's cost basis—35% below the IPO price, and more than 50% below its 52-week high—the presenter does not believe they are sellers anytime soon. The new fund’s basis is approximately today's price (a bit less than €9). Important to note, the presenter believes this is not comparable to ADT. ADT is a much worse business than Verisure for a few reasons. Verisure is completely vertically integrated with 40% market share. ADT uses an independent dealer network with inferior technology, and maintains a much lower market share (closer to 20%). This contributes to attrition that is more than double Verisure's, meaningfully weaker margins, and customer NPVs that are materially worse. And Verisure's markets have a far larger growth runway versus the nearly fully-penetrated US market.

The presenter thinks the predictability of the business lends itself to a DCF valuation. Using the presenter’s conservative base case, using an 8% discount rate, the stock could double from current levels and could compound to a triple over the next few years. The presenter thinks investors will better appreciate the company's business model, as its reinvestment rate reduces significantly in the coming quarters and its FCF generation becomes more obvious.

ideas.th: Not an AV loser: Level 4 players will need Uber's demand; 12x EBITDA vs 20x warranted, with above-Street 2027-28 EBITDA.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Uber as a long.

Uber has a $145 billion cap. It trades $1.5 billion per day. It is currently trading at 12x EBITDA (which is 6.5x turns below its historical three-year average).

This is not an AI loser or an AV loser. If you ride in a Waymo, Model X, an Aurora truck, or a Waabi semi, it will be clear that multiple players are going to get to Level 4+. Level 4+ is simply an industry term that means driver out, and no safety driver required in an autonomous vehicle. Uber has nearly 40 AV partners that are working towards this outcome, and the presenter thinks several of them are going to be successful in doing so. They have collectively committed to 120,000 AVs on Uber's network across those partners in the coming years.

NVIDIA is also helping. They have their own open-source platform, Alpamayo. Their incentive, by opening up an AV model, is obviously to sell GPUs into the assembly kit, but it gives autonomous capabilities to basically any OEM who wants to buy it. Componentry for AVs is also getting cheaper. The BOM (Bill of Materials) is lower by 50% to 75% over the last couple of years, depending whose estimates you look at. Lower cost components make it easier to get AV players to Level 4 and it also makes it more economical.

In terms of market share, Uber has 70% share of rides in the US. Here is a little context. Tesla has done two-and-a-half million total rides since launching last year (that is as of 2Q 2026). Waymo does 500,000 per week, Lyft does 20 million per week, and Uber does 45 to 60 million rides per week in the US.

Any of the players who crack Level 4 are going to want to go where the demand is, which is Uber. Behavior is hard to change, and Uber has a product that is more flexible than Elon's double-digit count of FSD robotaxis, because of the human driver. We all know Elon has walked back many AV claims, like incorporating the whole Tesla car park into the robotaxi fleet. He basically said the entire Tesla fleet would be capable of going into a robotaxi fleet—that if you have a Model X two years ago, you are going to bring it in, and you can have it go do rides for you at night when you are watching TV. He has obviously walked that back. To further that point, the presenter believes Uber's claim that they have gained share in the legacy AV markets of LA, San Francisco, and Phoenix, and it checks out in their data. Beyond the AV dynamics, the food delivery business has been growing healthily, with a stable to improving take-rate. The presenter also thinks the Delivery Hero deal is logical. On a pro forma basis, the presenter is mid-single digits above the Street on EBITDA in 2027 and is high-teens above the Street in 2028. The presenter thinks 20x is the right multiple for a fast-growing, profitable leader. This is where it traded prior to the AI/AV risk becoming mainstream. They also generate a lot of cash, and spend a lot on buybacks. So the presenter thinks investors get paid to fade the AI risk here.

ideas.th: Guide reset to beatable levels; weather-delayed demand, easier compares and pet bottoming drive comp inflection and re-rating from ~17x P/E.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Tractor Supply as a long after today's industry conference presentation. The stock was down 3.7% today, mainly, in the presenter’s opinion, driven by shorter-term duration investors who were thinking they would provide a quarter-to-date update, which they have not done over the past couple of events.

In terms of the setup, the stock started the year at $50, and traded as low as $29, before recovering to $34 over the past couple of months. In the presenter’s view, the stock was pretty much untouchable over the last year because of weak pet industry trends, as well as concerns over market share losses to Amazon, Chewy, Walmart, and the big mass retailers, which led to long-term investor capitulation.

But what makes it interesting now is that the presenter believes that full-year guidance was finally reset to a beatable level on the Q2 print. The full-year comp growth was cut to -1% to flat, from +1% to +3%, and that implies approximately -1.5% to slightly positive comp growth in the back half, despite significantly easier compares.

The current data implies that trends could end the quarter approximately 100 to 200 basis points ahead of the Street's -1% Q3 estimate. Compares then ease by approximately 360 basis points in Q4, and then they stay muted through the first half of 2027. So theoretically, the two-year math, you can extrapolate a return to low-single-digit and mid-single-digit comps by next quarter. That is in line with management's long-term algorithm, which to some extent, the presenter believes theyre iterated during today's conference presentation. So why have trends improved in recent months? The presenter thinks there are several different reasons. First, the presenter thinks the Q2 -1.5% comp growth was driven mainly by unfavorable weather back in May, and they commented on this during their last earnings call. What the presenter thinks you saw was a shifting of the spring selling season to later in the year, so you are simply delaying sales growth until this coming quarter, which is why the data seems to have accelerated quite meaningfully.

Second, the presenter thinks category trends are finally bottoming, to some extent. This is finally normalizing following COVID's excessive growth. It is important to remember that Tractor Supply's comp growth against 2019 is still one of the best in retail (approximately 6%). The presenter has also heard from several consumer staples companies like J M Smucker speak to improving pet trends in recent weeks, which is a good sign for the business. Third, company-specific initiatives, such as the push into pet animal services (which is growing at a faster rate), price investments funded by the tariff refunds, vendor rebates, as well as merchandise exchanges (for example, introducing Freshpet to the assortment), which have helped or are ramping up and are starting to help now.

And then lastly, commodity prices have become, or will likely become a big tailwind, with corn prices up approximately 25% over the last 12 months. It bodes well for an inelastic category (for example, the animal feed that they sell). And what the presenter has seen with names like Ulta Beauty, Target, and Dollar Tree is that comp growth inflections lead to significant multiple recovery. The company has historically traded between a range of 14x to 26x PE. It is currently trading approximately 17x PE (around the low end of the range). If comp growth is able to sustainably inflect to low to mid-singles for the next couple of quarters, the presenter would expect the stock to re-rate to low 20x, and then potentially higher if longer term investors start to revisit the name.

Additionally, this is a defensive name that is easier to own in this choppy macro environment with yields and oil prices rising. Ultimately, with improving top-line growth, it is a very favorable risk-reward. It screens as an attractive long, or a good hedge for a consumer short.

In terms of a price target, the presenter believes it is worth $40 to $45 (in the near term), and ultimately it could be worth $50 if investors revisit the name.

ideas.th: FRE/ALP nicotine pouches rolling out nationally; sales investment depresses 2026 EBITDA but run-rate returns to ~$120M at 25x.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Turning Point Brands as a long.

Turning Point Brands is a nicotine product and rolling paper company. It has a product portfolio that includes legacy brands Stoker's, which consists of snus and chew products, and Zig-Zag, which makes rolling papers, and a much faster growing set of products that are branded FRE and ALP (both nicotine pouch brands). That is the beginning, middle, and end of the thesis. The business is primarily focused on the nicotine pouch market. FRE is wholly owned by Turning Point. ALP is a 50/50 JV with Tucker Carlson. Turning Point does not have a combustible tobacco business.

In short, Turning Point is a compelling long opportunity because of its earnings growth outlook, which is supported by both secular tailwinds as well as market share gains. The company offers direct exposure to the nicotine pouch theme, simply as a percentage of the overall business mix. They have been on a tear for this past year. ALP and FRE have both been rolled out into national chains.

Historically this was not their sales tactic. Historically Turning Point would partner with independent stores, and effectively have sales people who sold out of their trunks. This year was a big step forward in terms of making a more institutionalized push, in terms of getting incremental market share and investing in marketing. They signed a deal with TKO earlier this year. They signed Conor McGregor as their European spokesperson. They are in the middle of this business transformation.

In terms of the legacy business, you have Stoker's and Zig-Zag, which pay a dividend and generate cash flow. Towards the end of 2025, the stock ran up materially (close to $140). The shares are currently trading around $74. The stock price ran up because you started to see the benefit of these independent chains and direct-to-consumer online marketplaces selling out their FRE and ALP products.

There was an intentional effort this year to invest more in sales and marketing. They are doing that, and there is a timing mismatch here. You run into contra revenue, stocking fees, slotting fees, etc. You also run into sales force productivity issues, where you are paying them up front and they slowly scale up.

This is a business that generated $120 million of EBITDA last year, will likely generate ~$80 million this year, and the presenter thinks it will run rate at the end of the year to around $120 million as well. If you give them credit for their old multiple (approximately 25x), for a business that is growing 20% to 30% per annum, you are looking at a business that the presenter thinks is worth closer to $140 to $150 per share over the next 12 months. If you are bullish on the nicotine pouch opportunity, although it is marketed as this de-risk product, ultimately it is bringing new folks into the category. You could reach a point by the end of the decade here where if they are able to get their 10% target market share, you are looking at $1 billion of pouch revenue. Now, obviously that is very assumption-rich, and you could do your own sensitivities around that. But the presenter thinks this is a very compelling opportunity, especially as a way to play the pouch theme.

In the presenter’s opinion, the biggest risk here is Tucker Carlson. The presenter’s view is that Turning Point’s regulatory headwinds will not be a punitive measure by the Trump administration, that the FDA will not be weaponized. Historically, Trump has been relatively pro-flavored vape and flavored nicotine pouch. It is really, the presenter thinks, a difficult case to make against Turning Point, but they think that is the principal risk here. They sell flavored pouches. ALP specifically sells a mint and a berry flavor. They do not sell vapes, but vapes have gotten approved by this FDA, so you could buy a berry vape, and that is a reduced risk product in the FDA's assertion.

ideas.th: Trough multiple as contracted media-rights step-ups kick in; Middle East event fears overdone and Zuffa boxing is an unmodeled call option.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss TKO as a long.

The presenter has a playbook in terms of what they are looking for in the consumer sector as potential longs They are looking for companies that fundamentally have printed well, with an elite management team, which deserve a premium multiple, but have traded poorly YTD and continue to do so.

In the presenter’s opinion, TKO sits at the intersection of short-term investors that are uncomfortable with the Middle East mix of promotional fee upside, as well as the event calendar. You saw Formula One had to cancel events. The presenter thinks a lot of investors who are long-term bulls in TKO want both incremental WWE as well as UFC site fees, and potentially more weekends spent in Jeddah or Riyadh, which they think is all fair. But if you take a step back, the stock has pulled back to a trough multiple on a forward basis at the exact moment when effectively all of their major media rights are now penciled in, including significant contractual step-ups. Those are going to start contributing in the back half and accelerate from there.

In terms of the setup, the stock is down 10% year over year, even though WWE has smashed sponsorship expectations (even versus the expectations of the perma bulls). The presenter thinks there is a little bit of uncertainty as it relates to the PSKY / HBO integration, and what does that mean if you really want to model your ratings reach on a UFC basis. But from the presenter's perspective, when you are buying it here, none of those factors are that relevant. Ultimately, they got a great step-up.

The presenter thinks Zuffa boxing is extremely interesting, so they want to come back to that as a potential third leg of the stool. You are looking at something that trades far cheaper than Formula One. The presenter thinks Ari and Mark, without question, are the best relationship managers in the business. If you really wanted to pound the table on the short thesis, media laggards are not going to buy sports, or some argument that there will not be upside for WWE’s next step-up, the presenter thinks Ari is going to take care of that.

Ultimately, the presenter thinks he has already shown that, frankly. If you just listen to what they are saying, this is a super conservative management team. They are always conservative. In Q1, they just beat-and-raised. The presenter is about to see the acceleration in the back half.

And if you look at Zuffa (their boxing promotion company), from the presenter's perspective at least, consumers have argued that there is an incremental sports league to be started—probably the best example being spring football. This is a business that already has all the contract workers in place, where they set up a ring on Friday for SmackDown, they can roll UFC Saturday, and you can see a world outside of football season where Sunday night becomes Zuffa night. It is not only not priced in, it is not even modeled. There is nobody on the Street trying to pencil out any form of actual math.

Zuffa is their version of attempting to create a WWE-style contract worker boxing media right that they can then sell. The business was formed as a 50% JV with Turki Al-Sheikh. They do not own all the upside but they also put in none of the capital risk up front. But what the presenter likes about it is it is not even part of the story / thesis at the moment. This is not like Formula One, where you hear people arguing about the undercard incremental races. No one is even bringing it up. WWE President Nick Khan is from Vegas. He is obsessed with boxing. Ari Emanuel is incredibly cagey about his ability to get stuff done. The presenter thinks there is a world in which they put on a decent amount of these fights next year, they become interesting, and then very quickly this becomes part of the story / thesis. If you were buying it at a fully priced forward multiple, it is a little bit harder to digest there. But the presenter thinks to own it here, it makes it super simple. That is call option upside.

If there is any sort of conclusion to the war, the stock rebounds effectively overnight, because people want more events in the Middle East because it has higher site fees. Globally, UFC is performing quite well. The presenter also thinks this is taking place at a talent trough. The presenter thinks there has not been a marketable Connor McGregor-type talent to market in a long time. Just the math would tell you, they will stumble their way into someone here. The presenter gets to a conservative base case / target price of $236, implying roughly 25% upside from current levels with limited downside. Investors are buying the stock near a trough multiple. On 2027 numbers, the presenter is at roughly 16x Adjusted EBITDA and 14x 2028 Adjusted EBITDA. Compared with Formula One, which the presenter would argue has a more complicated operating structure, it becomes a relatively clean story. You also have the LA Olympics in 2028, which the presenter thinks should be a major event for On Location. As you move through 2027, that should become a much bigger part of the story.

Does the presenter think this stock can double? Of course not. It is expensive and historically has been. But the presenter has seen that premium sports rights and live-event entertainment continue to command a bid. The presenter does not think the stock should be this caught up in Middle Eastern headline risk and believes the current multiple presents an interesting entry point.

ideas.th: Trough RV cycle at mid-cycle multiple; LCI merger adds $150M of likely conservative synergies and aftermarket mix.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Patrick Industries as a long.

For context, Patrick Industries is an upstream RV parts supplier. They are merging with the number two player in the industry, L CI Industries, and the deal is expected to close in the first half of next year.

The stock is currently trading at $77. Standalone, Patrick Industries has a $2.7 billion market cap and a $4 billion TEV. It has 35 million shares outstanding. Pro forma for the deal, the combined company would have a $5 billion market cap and a $7 billion TEV.

The presenter likes it for a few reasons. Number one, it is trading at a mid-cycle multiple, even on trough-ish earnings and a trough RV cycle. The stock is down 35% YTD. RV wholesale shipments have been guided down twice this year and are likely going to be under 300,000. This compares to a normalized number which is closer to 400,000. For context, shipments peaked at 600,000 during the pandemic.

Number two, you have $150 million of cost synergies that are likely conservative on a COGS base of $6 billion, and OPEX of $1.3 billion. That would add approximately $20 per share. And then the content per unit has been structurally growing. It has been from a combination of pricing as well as adding more value to the RV. Patrick focuses more on the interior of the RV, while L CI Industrials focuses more on the exterior of the RV. They have also been rolling up some of the smaller suppliers of those parts. So even though the RV industry is at trough, both companies have done a good job of compounding their top line.

Finally, the deal would increase the aftermarket exposure of the combined company. For Patrick Industries, only 10% of total revenue is derived from aftermarket while LCI Industries is closer to 30%. Important to note, aftermarket is higher margin. In terms of the pro forma valuation, they should be able to generate $1 billion of EBITDA, including synergies. The presenter has them generating a little over $1.2 billion by 2028, which does not assume a meaningful industry inflection and assumes RV units are 10% higher than they are currently. If you put a 9x multiple on that—it has historically traded in the 8x to 9x range—that equates to a $135 stock, with 75% upside from current levels.

ideas.th: Unit growth plus same-store pricing drive 15%+ EBITDA growth; PE selldown overhang is over and liquidity improved, yet only 9.5x EBITDA.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Life Time Group as a long.

For those not familiar with Life Time, it is the largest owner and operator of high-end fitness centers in the US. They own / operate approximately 200 centers today.

The stock has performed well year to date, but the presenter thinks it still has room to run, in terms of both the multiple and out-year earnings. The pitch is fairly simple. Their algo is very good. They are opening mid-teens of new centers per year, and that will likely go to the low 20s by 2030. But simply from opening new centers, you get more members, and those members add 5% to 6% to revenue over time.

They also have strong same-store sales growth. In recent years, it has been low double digits. This past quarter it was 9%. It will naturally come down to 5% or 6% over time. But same-store sales are driven by taking price on legacy members, as well as mix shift (when you have old members churn). When new members come in, the bench rate for new membership is much higher. Plus, people tend to sign up for more expensive plans like a family plan. And then in-store ancillary spend—personal training, Pilates or pickleball—everything else continues to grow very quickly.

Between the member growth and same-store growth, you get combined revenue growth of 11% or 12%. There is operating leverage on that. The presenter thinks you get to low-teens EBITDA growth over time. Today it is much better than that. In the presenter’s opinion, it will be 15% + through the end of this year and for all of 2027. So the presenter believes you have a great earnings algo.

Also worth noting, they have a phenomenal customer base. The presenter thinks thematically, you have a high-end customer, in a good category (health & wellness), and it is an “in-person” experience, which the presenter thinks are all areas within consumer that are showing great growth (a great thematic trend).

Their management is also viewed as very good operators. They beat and raise every single quarter, and the presenter thinks they finally figured out how to communicate with the Street, which should bode well for the stock.

It currently trades at only 9.5x EBITDA. If you look at the stock, it was $26 to start the year, and it is $42 currently. Important to note, there were two large overhangs on the stock coming into the year. The first was that fundamentally, if you looked at membership growth, it looked like it was growing low single digits, and investors thought they were taking a lot of price and that they could not grow members. That was largely because they were opening smaller centers and not as many centers in recent years. But, more so during the pandemic, they added a bunch of “qualified memberships.” These were members who were paying materially less. For example, these members were paying approximately $60 instead of $280, and now they are simply churning those people out. They are not letting them renew or they are forcing them out more aggressively. That is obviously very good for your mix, but it makes the blended membership rate look a lot lower when the core memberships are growing 4%, and as they add more centers in coming years, let us say you get the 5% or 6%. And then there was also a massive technical overhang on it. The stock was simply not very liquid. In the presenter’s opinion, investors knew Leonard Green and TPG were going to sell every single quarter. Now Leonard Green and TPG have gone from owning over 30% a few years ago to sub-5% combined today. They are essentially done selling. It trades over $100 million per day now. So it is finally liquid enough, and investors do not have to worry about secondaries.

And when the presenter looks at the rest of the Gaming, Leisure, & Lodging sector, they compare it to hotels and cruise lines. The C-corps are amazing businesses. They do not grow that fast. They are very expensive, and they have their own issues regarding fee concerns. Then cruise lines have a myriad of issues, and this trades closer to a cruise line, but you do not have to worry about oil. You do not have to worry about oversupply in the Caribbean, or low river levels in Europe. Even though Viking is a great stock, the presenter thinks Viking trades expensive relative to Life Time although it has a similar growth profile, and actually much more predictable growth for Life Time.

The presenter thinks now that it is more liquid, with memberships expected to increase, and they will likely beat and raise again starting this quarter (and every quarter for the foreseeable future), the presenter thinks it will attract more interest from investors who had viewed it as not liquid enough or had other concerns in the past.

As it relates to the technical dynamic, with PE selling down their stakes, this obviously increases the float, so you will get the next S&P rebalance in a few weeks. There has been a lot of selling over the past few months, which means there should be a material re-balancing for them. So, you could see a few hundred million dollars worth of passive flows—which is small, but it is helpful at the margin.

In terms of the presenter's price target, they think it could trade to 13x EBITDA—equivalent to a 1x EBITDA PEG ratio—which would equate to a $65 stock price using their 2027 EBITDA assumptions.

ideas.th: Higher rates and gas prices hit boat sales and usage-driven P&A (75% of EBIT) while Street expects both segments up.
ideas.cat: Weak Q3; possible Fed hike; Iran escalation
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Brunswick as a short.

In terms of the business, Brunswick sell sand maintains boats. The positive to this story is that most of the EBITDA or EBIT now comes from boat maintenance, but that has stopped growing, and has now been flat to declining. They will generate ~$350 million of EBIT this year, of which ~75% comes from their parts and accessories business (maintenance) and 25% is generated from their sales business. In the past, these two segments contributed closer to 50% each, but obviously given the decline in consumption and higher interest rates post-COVID, that has changed.

However, given what has gone on with interest rates and gas prices, the presenter thinks those two factors are having a fairly negative effect on boat sales. Boat sales are down 4% YTD, and the presenter suspects they will be even worse in the third quarter because of elevated gas prices. The presenter thinks you have a stock where there are expectations for both segments to be up year-over-year, and given sales are down along with elevated gas prices (the presenter believes people drove their boats less in the summer), there is likely going to be less P&A. If you put a historical multiple of ~12x EPS, that would equate to a stock in the $50s or $60s versus $70 today. And on EBITDA, you get a lot more because there is leverage on that.

The presenter's simple thesis is that this is a stock that has all the wrong factors (oil and interest rates). And if the Fed raises interest rates later this month, it is likely an incremental negative for them, because consumers tend to buy cars and boats on credit.

And from a macro / war standpoint, if you are Iran, they know that there is an election coming up in November. If you want to hurt Trump, this is the best chance to hurt him. The presenter believes that Iran will instigate, elevate, and escalate in October.

ideas.th: Record contract wins plus new Nexus data-center campus services scaling to $1B+ revenue by 2028.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Aramark as a long.

Aramark is a leading global provider of food and facilities services to education, health care, business and industry, sports, leisure, and corrections clients; more recently they have entered the data center market. The largest market is the United States, with a 15-country footprint outside of that which comprises their international segment.

Aramark manages interrelated services, food, and hospitality procurement for school districts, colleges, universities, and health care. These are sticky businesses that are all very profitable, so the presenter would argue that the risk of contract infringement or anything like that is pretty low.

There are two reportable segments. They have a US and International segment. The US is approximately 70% while International is the remaining 30%. And within the US, they have the five different segments that the presenter mentioned earlier. They have been generating organic sales growth of mid-single digit plus, accelerating over the last couple of years in the +7% to +9% range. Over the last four quarters, they have added major contracts within all verticals. The Healthcare segment in particular added two significant new customers. They added UPenn Medicine, which is approximately 4,000 beds (which is how they typically measure contracts), and then they added RWJBarnabas Health, which is another 5,700 beds. Those were their two largest contracts ever.

And then in sports and leisure, they have won Stone Mountain, Georgia, which is a resort, Texas State Athletics, FSU, and then Oklahoma and Alabama Departments of Corrections. In education, they have added Texas State, Grand Canyon University, Colorado Springs, and some other big businesses like Paul Weiss, Toyota, Discovery, and Blue Origin. Year to date, they have added approximately $1.6 billion in new client wins. They have averaged adding ~$600 million per quarter in new business.

Then in April (this is what the presenter believes is exciting to investors), they have added a new business segment called Nexus, which consists of their data center management service. When all these data centers are being built, Aramark will build campuses with gyms, dining rooms, and various facilities to make it enjoyable for the workers constructing the data centers, and there are a number of these data centers being built at the moment. They build a campus right next to it where everyone is housed, and then they are managing those facilities. It is pre and post construction. The contracts are typically four to five years. Data centers are typically built in two to four years, give or take, so this is a big point of expansion.

Each per capita is approximately $40,000 to $45,000 per head, so they are meaningful contracts. They average about $140 to $160 million per year. They just started ramping, so the contribution this year will be minimal, but they should get to north of $500 million next year. The presenter has them doing a little over $1 billion in 2028. Then in 2029, the presenter has them well over $1.5 billion. The scaling is pretty fast.

They are working with three hyperscalers currently and three individual data centers, but each of those hyperscalers have several different data centers—between 7 and 12 each—so the presenter believes the ability to add within those three clients is pretty strong. You can see them generating well over $2 billion down the road by 2030 if that happens. The presenter has them generating ~$2.2 billion of EBITDA in FY 28. If you put a conservative 11x multiple on that, you can get to a $77 target price. The presenter believes the multiple has room to expand to 12x to 13x. Some of the Street analysts are giving them a 13.5x multiple, which the presenter thinks is a little rich, but 12x to 13x would equate to an $85 or $90 target price.

ideas.th: 800G+ transceiver volumes doubling and 1.6T mix lift TIA/driver ASPs; $10 EPS power vs ~$6 consensus with cellular divestiture lifting margins.
ideas.cat: Cellular module divestiture; CopperEdge hyperscaler deployment
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Semtech as a long.

Semtech is a diversified supplier of analog mixed-signal components. Approximately 35% of the business is related to signal integrity (housing its high-growth FiberEdge, CopperEdge business). Another 35% lies within its protection, sensing, and wireless products. The remaining 30% is related to various IoT assets. The presenter believes you will see significant upside from that signal integrity business that houses the fiber and connectivity solutions. First, within signal integrity, Semtech holds assets utilized in transceivers, such as TIAs and drivers. Semtech should benefit materially from the upcoming transceiver cycle. First, the overall volume of high-speed transceivers should see significant growth. The presenter thinks the market is coming from a base of 80 to 90 million 800 G and up transceivers this year to 160 to 180 million in 800 G next year—so that is roughly a double in terms of volume. The second part is, within that mix, you have more products shifting to the next-generation 1.6T transceivers. The presenter believes those next-generation transceivers can offer ASPs up to 50% to 100% higher versus the 800-gig generation for their TIA products. Within the transceiver mix specifically, the presenter expects 1.6T volume to grow from approximately 20% of the mix to just under 50%, which offers pricing upside.

And on top of that, in the next generation, Semtech should maintain strong share. Along with the organic growth as well, they made a recent acquisition of HieFo, which expands their SAM within the transceiver module market and gives them assets and a roadmap to attack the emerging NPO/CPO opportunities.

Outside of the FiberEdge business, you also can look at the copper assets. There should be growth within their linear equalizer business, which is utilized to extend the reach of copper cables. Semtech's products should be deployed by a major hyperscaler—presumably Google—and there is further upside if Nvidia utilizes this technology in future improvement designs. They are also in negotiations with other partners, so it remains to be seen how that business progresses.

Outside of this broader connectivity portfolio, Semtech is also in the process of realigning its product portfolio, and they are in the end stages of divesting this cellular module business. The presenter believes this could likely add a few hundred basis points to gross margin. So as the mix shifts to more of the signal integrity business, you have a pathway to go from a high-50%s gross margin to mid-60%s longer term.

Net-net, while supply constraints remain a key risk for this industry, the presenter sees a pathway for signal integrity to roughly double versus what consensus is currently modeling. The presenter is underwriting $10 of EPS power in a few years as consensus is closer to $6. Even applying a low-20s multiple, which is slightly below their historical average but slightly above broader networking peers, you get to approximately 60% upside from today’s stock price. And if you really dream the dream on the module, on the CopperEdge side, you can easily see the stock doubling. The presenter thinks the downside from here is likely only 25% or 30%. So they think the risk-reward skew is pretty attractive at these levels.

ideas.th: Tower REIT at ~14x AFFO is a year from AMT-like organic growth and likely remains an M&A target for American Tower.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss SBA Communications as a long.

SBA is a communications infrastructure / tower company. It is trading at approximately 14x AFFO per share. It has an $18 billion market cap and a $35 billion EV.

From a risk-reward perspective, what the presenter is talking about as far as its multiple range—if you look at spreads versus the 10-year, it can range anywhere from 13x to 18x; so, investors are pretty optimistic on this company.

The presenter would argue that the aspect to the story that investors are not appreciating is that they are approximately a year away from having an organic growth opportunity that looks very similar to the largest tower peer in the space, American Tower, who has laid out plans for mid-single-digit top-line organic / mid-to-high-single-digits bottom-line growth. The presenter believes that SBAC is an M&A target, specifically from American Tower. The stock was trading at $170; then there were reports that it was in M&A talks and the stock subsequently traded to $210; then press reports indicated the M&A talks were over, so the stock is now trading in the high $170s. The presenter thinks those talks are likely still ongoing in some way, shape, or form.

In summary, the presenter thinks you have an attractive risk/ reward skew here. The upside on a deal is not simply the 20% to 25% you might get from multiple normalization plus positive earnings in 2028, but you also have another 25% to 50% M&A premium that could come in. Also worth noting, it is not involved at all with the AI complex, so you do not need to worry about Nvidia announcing $500 billion of financing and what that means. It should be considered a relatively safe long.

ideas.th: Post-print US DAU selloff overdone; unique human content, ~60% revenue growth at ~12.5x EV/EBITDA, AI licensing renewals to come.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Reddit as a long.

This stock is extremely controversial. It has enormous, inordinate volatility, in the presenter's opinion. But when the presenter looks at this company, they do not see any other comparable property that has the same dimension of human content.

In terms of the setup, the stock sold off dramatically after they reported earnings on July 30th. The stock went out at $180 the night before; it was trading around $140 the next morning. So what caused the move? Their DAUs went down by approximately 200,000 in the US, while their international user growth was strong. So the fear is that user growth in the US is flattening out.

The other controversy regarding the stock is over their renewal with Google and their licensing agreement, where Google pays approximately $60 million this year, and there is talk that they were asking for $120 million. In terms of the magnitude of what Google and the other AI companies are spending on CAPEX, the renewal amount is insignificant. The presenter thinks that the overhang on the stock surrounding the renewal of the licensing agreement was blown out of proportion. Eventually, the presenter thinks there will be an agreement with Google, followed by OpenAI, and then Anthropic (because they are trying to sue them).

But what you have here is a company with 194 million shares outstanding, a $28 billion EV, that is going to generate $1.5 billion of EBITDA this year, going to $2 billion next year. You are talking 12.5 times enterprise value. There is some stock comp in there that is not insignificant, but this business has no CAPEX. Its revenue is growing 60%. It generate san enormous amount of cash flow. They bought back $250 million worth of stock in the quarter. They generate more content in one month than the entire Wikipedia library. The presenter believes that if you are Google or OpenAI, you are going to want to have access to this content. The controversy is that no one is going to go to Reddit, that they are simply going to go to Reddit via Google, and those subscribers are not as valuable. The presenter does not think that is going to happen, because there is still enormous growth internationally. Their ARPU growth is extraordinary.

ideas.th: Vineland NJ 250MW buildout blocked by city council puts ~$2.9B of the $7-9B YE ARR target at risk while $20B+ of debt is needed.
ideas.cat: Aug 17 city council vote; 45-day appeal; Q2 earnings
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Nebius as a short.

For those not familiar with it, it is a neocloud. What is a neocloud? It depends on who you ask. They are either an NVIDIA GPU reseller, or they are a play on the future of the public cloud, where enterprises are going to be renting out dedicated GPU capacity in the same way that they do from the hyperscalers today. If the market remains significantly compute constrained long-term, these players have a place in the market.

The reason why the presenter thinks it is a short is that Nebius has a $7 to $9 billion ARR target for the end of this year. They have approximately 16 data center sites under contract, but the most critical one for this year is in Vineland, New Jersey. Vineland is going to house a Microsoft contract for them, where they will get approximately $17.4 billion over the next five years. On 300 megawatts at that site, it implies about $11.6 million of ARR per megawatt.

They have delivered 50 megawatts at that site—so 50 of the 300—and they are currently facing community backlash around being able to stand up the incremental 250 by the end of the year. A week ago, there was a city council meeting to vote on whether or not Nebius can stand up the rest of the 250, and it ended in a “no” vote. The next meeting is August 17th. Presumably, there will be another vote then. Even if that occurs, there is a 45-day appeals process, which puts you out to October 1st, if all goes well, to when they can start standing up these 250 megawatts.

The partner at the site is Bloom Energy. Bloom Energy has touted their ability to stand up 55 megawatts in 55 days for Oracle, as one of the fastest deployments they have ever done. If you do the math based on October 1st to the end of the year, it does not get to the 250 that they would need. So at $11.6 million of ARR per megawatt, the presenter believes you have $2.9 billion of that $7 to $9 billion ARR target at risk. Even if they get half of that, it is still a problem for the range, because they are assuming that it is fully stood up in the guide. So where could you be wrong? There has been some speculation that you could get a large deal announcement with Anthropic on the quarter this Wednesday. Candidly, they have two over-one-gigawatt sites that are contracted—not yet built, but contracted—that investors have been speculating that Anthropic could come in and fill. But, in the presenter’s opinion, if you ask anyone how they are modeling this business, no one puts those sites in their model without anyone filling that capacity long-term. So you need to believe that Anthropic is going to sign a meaningfully upsized deal relative to what the current market rate is on a dollars per megawatt basis.

There has also been some speculation that they could sign a deal with Google for one of those full gigawatt sites. Over the weekend, there were some rumors circulating on X that suggested that it would be a $33 billion deal over five years. That is highly problematic when you back into the implied dollars per megawatt (it is approximately $7 million per megawatt). The base is currently run-rating at $10 to $11 million. The Microsoft contract is worth about $11.5 million per megawatt.

So the question is, why would they do that? It is because they know they need to raise over $20 billion plus in debt over the next year that the market likely would rebuke, when you look at what is going on with hyperscaler CDS spreads and the Bitcoin miners. If they were to sign a deal like that, it would signal a lot of desperation. And the presenter does not think this is the type of stock that can work when numbers get cut, especially when there are terminal value concerns.

In terms of price target, the presenter believes that there is 25% downside from current levels based on DCF derived values from future contracted cash flows.

ideas.th: Bumble is failing as Match outspends it 5x; once it exits, pricing and buybacks lift EPS growth to ~15% and the 11x P/E re-rates.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Match Group as a long.

Everybody knows what the company does. They have Hinge and Tinder. They compete with Bumble. The pitch comes down to the balance sheets and what is changing on the balance sheets. This company has an $8.5 billion market cap, and they have bought back $1 billion of stock in the last six quarters. Their competitor, Bumble, has a $700 million EV, and most of that is debt. And Bumble is really holding on for dear life right now—the stock is currently trading at $2.

The pitch comes down to the fact that the presenter thinks Bumble is going to be gone soon, and when and if that turns out to be true, Match will be a compelling long. It has not been a good long, as it has gone through a series of different CEOs. If you go back over the last 15 years, every three to four years it cycles to a new CEO. The presenter thinks the current CEO is good. He came from Zillow, Spencer Rascoff.

He is fixated on engagement, and you can start to see that in the metrics that are available through third parties. And the real visibility of that is, Bumble is failing. For reference, Match generates $3.5 billion in revenues while Bumble only generates $800 million in revenues, so four-to-one. And then Match outspends Bumble five to one in terms of marketing dollars. The presenter believe sit does not really matter who is on the app six months ago; what matters is who is coming onto the app tomorrow. And Match is outspending Bumble by 5x. You can see the engagement metrics, number of visits, minutes per visit—both of those are declining at Bumble. Whereas at Match and Tinder, they are growing, both those sets of metrics, and that is what the CEO of Match is fixated on.

Match’s growth is approximately 4% or 5%, but that is not the bet that you are making here. The bet is the P/E multiple, which is 12.5x this year and 11x next year, and that Bumble goes away and they start to modestly increase prices (across all their various tiers). For example, you hit this button for gold status, which enables you to download more photos. They have done a tremendous job on these initiatives in the past, which they are not talking about at the moment, because the presenter thinks their likely goal is to make sure Bumble is gone. Once Bumble is gone, then they can start to tweak things on the platform. And if there are only two apps you can download—one is more serious while the other is more casual—you have a lot of flexibility. That is the bet that the presenter is making.

If that happens, the buyback, which they are buying at a higher and higher price point—the presenter gave you the number earlier—they have bought 32 million shares at roughly $33 per share; the stock is at $37. But if you study the prices that they are buying at most recently, most recently in July, they bought it at $40, and the stock just dropped. So they have been active buyers at these levels, and they are retiring a decent amount of stock.

The bet is that pricing starts to lift from 4% to approximately 7% to 8%, and you get some margin accretion because they do not need to spend much on marketing. You should get an increase in the buyback, with EPS growth that looks more like +15%, and they are the only game in town. If that happens, then the presenter thinks the P/E multiple starts to shift, because the EPS right now, right here, it would look like 8x or 9x next year's EPS, in which case they think investors are likely willing to pay 14x to 15x for a company that is growing +8% to +9% with a decent visibility.

The presenter is not telling you it is a phenomenal industry. But what they have seen is, sometimes you get phenomenal stocks in industries that are not doing well, as competitors go away. Bumble is not going away tomorrow, but investors should keep it on their radar. The presenter thinks if they continue getting additional third-party data points that Bumble is about to fold, Match should work from the long side.

ideas.th: Silvus mesh-radio and D-Fend drone businesses growing 20-25% under conservative guidance; sees $25 2028 EPS vs Street $21.
ideas.cat: Anduril IPO; continued guidance raises on Silvus
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Motorola Solutions as a long.

Motorola Solutions has a $77 billion market cap, an $87 billion EV, and trades approximately $1 billion per day.

Motorola Solutions unifies communications, video, and security technology to protect people, property, and places across public safety and businesses. Approximately two-thirds of their business is used by first responders—such as ambulances, critical infrastructure, and communications within state and local municipalities.

The pitch is that in one-third of their business, revenues are growing approximately 20% to 25% due to recent acquisitions (this is separate from their stable LMR radio business, which is the critical infrastructure segment of their business that is growing low single digits with high margins and a sticky customer base with long-term contracts). The growth segment is in what is called mesh radio networks, which is used for drone technologies.

For example, one of the growth angles to the story that the presenter thinks will get picked up by investors when Anduril Industries eventually goes public, is that this software is essentially on (the presenter estimates) two-thirds of Anduril's devices.

In addition, them anagement team is very conservative. Every quarter they have been guiding up the acquisition of Silvus Technologies that closed approximately a year ago. They have what is called a “self-healing network”, meaning that if one of the local networks goes down, they can incorporate the other devices on the network and essentially be their own local network. That business is growing 25% per year, and every quarter they have guided those numbers higher.

The Street is assuming $21 per share of earnings in 2028. The presenter thinks they can generate $25 per share of earnings, between this deal and this other acquisition called D-Fend Solutions, which is a drone-capture technology, where they can essentially hack any drones that are in an area, and instead of shooting them down, they can essentially take them over and land them safely. That business is also growing mid-20%s at 50% EBITDA margins. That is where their variance comes from versus the Street and where their management is very conservative on these assumptions. They are currently supply constrained on all these products, but they are building facilities and have doubled their sales staff to meet this demand.

In summary, they have a customer base that is very sticky, with long-term contracts and high margins.

ideas.th: Contracted Google/Nvidia-backed leases worth $75-130/sh vs $86; Texas regulatory fear overdone and River Bend expansion coming.
ideas.cat: River Bend expansion; Texas regulatory clarity around November election
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Hut 8 as a long.

For background, the company has announced three contracts, which equate to $1.75 billion of NOI, with a third of it backed by Google and two-thirds backed by Nvidia. If you do a DCF of the lease payments, it is $75, and if you put a cap rate on it, it is $130. For reference, the stock is currently trading at $86.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes there is a little bit of regulatory uncertainty based on the governor of Texas. And the presenter believes if Texas has problems with data centers, every other single pitch that is tied to data centers today would be trading lower than where they are currently trading.

In the presenter’s opinion, the Batch Zero processes that are funded by the biggest companies in the world, that have debt financing, that are going to be completed by great operators, are going to be approved. Two-thirds of the leases that the presenter mentioned, those that generate the $1.75 billion of NOI, come from the Batch Zero process, from the Corpus Christi asset of Hut 8. It is called the Beacon Point asset.

The presenter thinks that if this issue did not exist, the stock would be $20 or $30 higher. Investors have made a lot of money in it, so you have some investors taking profits. The presenter thinks this is an exceptional risk-reward, where you can deploy real capital and sleep at night knowing that you are going to make money. How much money obviously depends on how great the AI trade plays out from here.

But they have a River Bend facility where they are getting more power from Entergy, and the presenter believes Entergy wants to see some behind-the-meter investment by Hut 8, while Entergy invests to generate some of that power generation. Hut 8, the presenter believes, by the end of this year will announce an expansion of the River Bend project, which should be equal to what they have already announced in River Bend.

You should also get clarity in Texas—after the November election if not beforehand - via press releases, etc. In terms of the analyst community, one sell-side analyst’s price target, which does not give them full value for everything in the pipeline but gives enough value, is $250. The stock is currently trading at $86. The presenter thinks what has been announced, plus River Bend, plus behind the meter, should get them to a $150 price target.

And the presenter feels that the Situational Awareness unwind, the AI selloff, plus this Texas aspect, have put investors in a position where you can buy any Bitcoin miner and feel excited about the setup. You could buy Riot, and if they lease all of Corsicana it is probably worth $30-plus, but they have not really executed on much besides 25 megawatts to AMD. Core Scientific has done a lot of work with CoreWeave, but they have not announced too much, and their execution has been questioned by investors.

The presenter believes that the companies that have repeatedly delivered / executed for institutional investors are Hut 8 and Terawulf. Terawulf has announced contracts worth $17 to $19, and it is trading at $17 to $19 (the presenter believes it is still a good setup). Hut 8 has announced contracts likely worth $120, and they are likely going to announce additional positive updates, and they are viewed as good executors. The presenter feels like Hut 8 is likely the best risk-reward out of the group.
