ideas.th: Bedrock monetizes multi-model inference tied to Anthropic/OpenAI ARR at higher margins, with room to raise compute pricing; 22x $18 2028 EPS.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Amazon.com as a long.

The presenter acknowledges that this is not a controversial call, but the way they are thinking about it currently is, there is still a lot of upside even after this move. The presenter knows it is not up a lot on a year to date basis, but it is up a lot post-CY 2Q earnings. The presenter believes it is worth $400 in the near term (EPS of $18 in 2028 using a 22x multiple, which equates to a $400 target price).

The piece to the story that the presenter is excited about is the piece that they think investors are starting to come around to, which is Bedrock. It is a smaller part of the AWS AI platform. The presenter has always thought frontier model—frontier, frontier, frontier - open source does not matter. The presenter thinks in the last six months to nine months, it has become clearer that, whether it is going to be open source or not, companies are more committed to being multi-model, meaning they want to be able to use Anthropic or OpenAI, or they might also want to bring in Kimi or some of the other open-source models.

So the presenter has been trying to figure out ways to express that view. They think there are a few business models in the private markets to express this view like Baseten, Fireworks, and some of the other inference clouds. In the presenter's view, the best way, at least at their scale, to express the view that companies are going multi-model is through the cloud providers. Particularly, each one of them has a version of this - Bedrock, Foundry, and Vertex—that is for Amazon, Microsoft, and Google respectively. For reference, Bedrock's is much larger.

At the end of the day, you have a line in the Amazon business model and in the Microsoft-Google business model that is tied directly to Anthropic and OpenAI's ARR growth, because some percentage of the tokens accessed for Anthropic and OpenAI are being accessed through Bedrock, Foundry, and Vertex. That has started showing up in terms of revenue growth—it is the CAPEX converting to revenue growth—but also it is showing up in terms of higher EBIT margins, because these token-as-a-service products that are offered through Bedrock come at a marginally higher EBIT margin, which is also good for the business. The presenter does not have a view on Nebius or CoreWeave—but this is their differentiated worldview on Amazon that gets them excited. If you do the rough math on the numbers that are out there—for Anthropic as an example, and this is likely a conservative number that investors are talking about—but if they end the year at $100 billion of ARR and they have two or three gigawatts of compute, that means they are monetizing that compute at $50 billion per gigawatt (you can do it on megawatts, but let us just say $50 billion per gigawatt). The cloud providers are currently charging between ~$10 to $12 billion per gigawatt to rent that compute space, so the presenter estimates the labs are doing 80% to 90% inference margins.

It probably does not stay that high, but to the presenter, that is an exciting thing happening in the market. The end consumers of labs are growing what they are able to monetize at faster than the clouds are scaling their price. The presenter does not know how to conceptualize it, but there is certainly room for the clouds to raise their price, particularly when Anthropic and OpenAI are scooping up every bit of compute. And then there is a spillover into the marginal suppliers of compute, like the Nebiuses and CoreWeaves. The presenter has not thought enough about that yet.

But to the presenter, if your main customer is earning somewhere upwards of 80% margins, there is probably room for that cost to go up. That is another pricing lever on the cloud businesses that gets the presenter excited in terms of their longer-term view. They do think investors have come around to the fact that the CAPEX they are spending is producing faster revenue growth, but there are other levers that are exciting.

The presenter would like to discuss Astera Labs as a long.

The company specializes in designing high-speed connectivity solutions for data centers and AI infrastructure. The whole idea is that if you continue to connect clusters, you need more scale-up switch. And surprisingly, there is no merchant in scale up switch. Right now you have some competitors in the space like Broadcom, but the presenter thinks that a lot of these customers buying other XPUs do not want to be beholden to Broadcom, where traditionally they were not a great supplier to many of these customers.

The presenter thinks if they can grow above mid-teens in EPS next year, and possibly above $30 to $35 in 2028, it is a stock that should re-rate as it comes more into the public view, outside of being what is viewed as a niche semiconductor coverage name at the moment.

ideas.th: Jeol holds >50% share in spot e-beam tools needed for indium phosphide lasers, not in Street numbers; mid-teens P/E vs Aixtron 30x.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Jeol Ltd. as a long.

The presenter likens Jeol to the ASML of optical. The presenter would also argue that it is cheap on an absolute and relative basis, and that the company is not well followed by investors.

The presenter believes it is a high-quality company. Their long-term operating margins are somewhat in the 40% range for their industrial segment, which is the segment the presenter cares about. They also have a really deep R&D moat, so they are not an over-earning commodity type business or anything like that.

For reference, the ticker is 6951 JP. It is a Japanese company. They have roughly a $2.5 billion market cap. Just for context, in terms of the stock and the fundamentals, they have been roughly steady—not explosive growth or anything like that—in the past few years. This is in part because their core businesses are more so tied to tools that make EUV masks. They are more levered to SKU count as opposed to volumes. It could be analogous to EDA, so that is why the business has been somewhat steady.

But the hidden gem and the crux of the thesis is that they have a front-end tool that every optical company—like Lumentum, Coherent, & Dongshan—needs to create indium phosphide and also CW (ultra-high-power lasers). From all their checks, it is clear that companies are increasing CAPEX and trying to expand capacity (the presenter believes approximately greater than 5x for this indium phosphide over the next five years). The question is, how do you play this theme through picks and shovels? This is one way you can do it. The market, it seems like they have already discovered the Lam of optical, which the presenter would argue is Aixtron in Germany, which trades at a hefty multiple (30x calendar 2027 EPS). But the market is missing the opportunity to invest in JEOL, which the presenter believes is the ASML of optical, and only trades at a mid-teens multiple on calendar 2027 EPS. The presenter believes that practically no optical revenue is baked into Street assumptions / numbers.

So the part that the presenter really cares about for JEOL is the spot e-beam tool. What that does is, it uses super precise electron beams to physically carve the gradients on the indium phosphide lasers. For reference, tool demand scales with how many lasers you want to create. This is exactly what benefits companies like Coherent and others.

The presenter would note, in this market for spot e-beam tools, this company has greater than 50% share. And then from the presenter's bottoms-up work with indium phosphide, it seems like the market will need greater than 300 tools over the next few years (call it $3 million per for these tools). So all in, this might add 10% to 20% top-line growth on top of what the Street has assumed, simply from this segment alone, which is the segment that the presenter cares about.

Again, the Street is assuming very minimal growth for this company overall, call it low-single-digit, mid-single-digit percent growth. The presenter thinks it could be 10% to 15% above that, just from the spot e-beam. Based on a fair multiple—25x calendar 2027—and using the presenter's numbers, the stock should be a double from here. The hidden gem is the spot e-beam. They literally help you create more indium phosphide. They are a toolmaker that can participate in that.

[2026-07-29] We had VIRT Long discussed earlier this month, with an investor citing a shift from buybacks toward balance-sheet investment, rising retail trading activity, and new opportunities from prediction markets, perpetual futures, and 24/7 trading as drivers to growth for the company.

ideas.th: Sees the stock as well positioned to benefit in agentic ecommerce
ideas.pitch:
[2026-07-27] We had PYPL Long most recently discussed in March with an investor seeing the stock as well positioned to benefit in agentic ecommerce as it provides merchants and customers the ability to identify each other when an agent is the one interacting.

[2026-07-29] We have had PYPL Long discussed various times over the years and while the company has been improving, many metrics still sit below investor expectations as the company works to improve margins, and branded checkout growth.

[2026-07-29] Beyond this, the company expects agentic payments, PayPal World, advertising, and digital identity to become more meaningful from 2028 onward, which lines up with the most recent views we had on the name.

[2026-08-04] We had PYPL Long discussed in March with a similar view as an investor saw Paypal providing key merchant and customer data to help with agentic ecommerce and the identification of buyers and sellers given its large existing network of customers.

[2026-08-28] We had PYPL Long discussed earlier this year with an investor offering a positive view for the company as it gains importance with AI that will require more knowledge about buyers and sellers in a agentic world.

[2026-09-22] On top of this, there was discussion during this PYPL Long, which saw the company well positioned to benefit from agentic shopping as merchants need to be able to identify shoppers and verify purchase ability.
